articles.title: Raised by a tough father, Captain Mark Phillips, who rarely praised her, Zara Tindall says she is trying to parent her children differently
articles.summary: Zara Tindall, Olympic silver medallist and granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II, knows what it’s like to grow up under high expectations.
articles.body: Zara Tindall, Olympic silver medallist and granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II, knows what it’s like to grow up under high expectations. Both her parents, Princess Anne and Captain Mark Phillips, were Olympic equestrians. You’d think that would set a pretty daunting standard. But for Zara, the real pressure didn’t come from her royal ties; it came from her parents’ focus on hard work, discipline, and a drive for excellence. Especially her father’s coaching style shaped her understanding of success, and now, it’s helping her decide how she wants to parent her own kids.When Zara, a mother of three and the British Olympic silver medallist, looks back, she remembers a childhood packed with horses, chores, and a constant effort to live up to her father’s demanding standards. Recently, on the Talk Horse podcast, she candidly shared how tough her father could be. Praise from him? Incredibly rare. For a young girl, a simple “Yeah, that was good” felt almost impossible to earn. His expectations forced her to keep aiming higher; she admits she always wanted that elusive approval, even when it seemed just out of reach.Princess Anne, on the other hand, took a more laid-back approach, offering encouragement and letting Zara push at her own pace. The contrast wasn’t lost on Zara. One parent gently nudged, the other gave direct, sometimes blunt instructions for improvement.Growing up under a strict parentPart of growing up with that level of intensity meant having responsibilities that went well beyond the royal image outsiders might imagine. Zara and her brother, Peter, had barn chores like anyone else. They cleaned tack, mucked out stables, and spent their free time immersed in the practical side of equestrian life. There was no easy route or special treatment just because of their family name. For Zara, that was a lesson in earned respect, one that’s deeply influenced how she sees effort and accomplishment."My father was quite critical. Very rarely you would get a, 'Yeah, that was good' out of him. So it was always striving to try and get that comment," she said, describing him as a "tough coach".For a young athlete, constantly trying to earn a parent's approval can be a demanding experience.On the other hand, " Mum's very relaxed," Zara recalled, explaining that her mother would encourage her to simply do what she could. Her father's approach, however, was more direct, with instructions to do more, improve further and correct what was not working.From a demanding childhood to Olympic successHer parents’ backgrounds helped set the tone. Captain Mark Phillips wasn’t just some authoritative father; he was a gold-medal-winning Olympic rider for the British eventing team in 1972. Princess Anne broke new ground herself as the first royal to compete in the Olympics, representing Great Britain in Montreal in 1976. Growing up at Gatcombe Park, surrounded by horses, Zara and her brother learned early on that achievement in equestrian sport had to be backed by commitment and genuine grit. Her parents made it clear: the doors might open, but only hard work would keep them open.All of this molded Zara into a serious competitor. Her breakthrough came in 2006 at the World Equestrian Games in Aachen, Germany, when she won individual gold, which is a feat that made her one of Britain’s top equestrians and earned her the BBC Sports Personality of the Year award. Then, at the 2012 London Olympics, she added a team silver medal, handed to her by her own mother, Princess Anne, in a memorable family moment. While she credits her father’s tough coaching with preparing her for the realities of elite competition, she acknowledges that sometimes it felt overwhelming.Why Zara Tindall is trying to be a gentler parent to her three childrenNow, as a mother of three, Zara finds herself thinking about all of this, where it helped her, where it left her wanting something different. She shares three children with her husband, former England rugby international Mike Tindall. Their daughters, Mia Grace, 12, and Lena Elizabeth, eight, and their son, Lucas Philip, five, are growing up surrounded by horses, competition, family tradition, and the same sporting environment that shaped their mother's childhood.On the podcast, she described a recent moment with her eldest daughter, Mia. She offered a bit of riding advice; Mia rolled her eyes. The funny thing? Zara realized she’d given the same advice to her nieces, who took it in stride. Clearly, there’s a generational pattern here, one she recognizes from her own childhood, raising a smile even as she tries to approach things differently than her father did.Zara is honest about the pressure she felt growing up. She doesn’t deny that her father’s critical edge built her resilience, and she’s grateful for the work ethic it instilled. But with her own kids, she’s making a conscious choice to hold back a bit. She wants to push them to do their best, sure, but not to the point where they feel approval is a prize they might never win. She knows too well what it’s like to crave a parent’s positive word, and how easy it is to let those high expectations come to define you.Breaking the cycle: Can parents be ambitious without being overly critical?This is a challenge that many parents face, not just those in the public eye. When does discipline cross the line into unnecessary pressure? How do you nurture ambition without making your child think their effort is never enough? Zara seems to be choosing a more compassionate path. She wants her children to understand the rewards of hard work, but she’s just as determined to show them that encouragement and recognition matter, too.And if Mia’s eye rolls are proof, the next generation won’t be shy about telling her when enough advice is enough. It’s a balancing act: carrying forward the best parts of what you were given, while letting go of the burdens that shouldn’t have to be passed on. For Zara Tindall, it’s about building a family legacy that isn’t just about winning medals, but about raising kids who love what they do and feel good about who they are, no matter what score the judges give.You use AI every day. articles.title: New York Marathon 2026 Route, Course Map, Times, Road Closures & Event Details
articles.summary: The 2026 TCS New York City Marathon will bring tens of thousands of runners and spectators to the streets of New York on Sunday, November 1. The 26.2-mile race travels through all five boroughs, starting on Staten Island and finishing in Manhattan's Central Park.
articles.body:
The 2026 TCS New York City Marathon will bring tens of thousands of runners and spectators to the streets of New York on Sunday, November 1. The 26.2-mile race travels through all five boroughs, starting on Staten Island and finishing in Manhattan's Central Park.

This year's event has particular significance: New York Road Runners (NYRR) is celebrating the 50th anniversary of the five-borough marathon route. The 2026 edition also introduces a minor but notable course adjustment in the Bronx, making it important for returning runners and spectators to check the latest map before race day.

Whether you're participating, supporting a runner, watching from the sidelines or simply trying to navigate the city, here's everything you need to know about the 2026 New York City Marathon.

Start location: Fort Wadsworth, Staten Island

Finish location: Central Park, Manhattan

The event begins with staggered starts throughout the morning, allowing runners to depart in five waves.

The 2026 race follows its traditional five-borough course. It starts at Ford Wadsworth on Staten Island, crosses the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge into Brooklyn, continues through Queens and the Bronx, and eventually returns to Manhattan for the finish in Central Park.

One of the most important changes to this year's marathon is the adjusted Bronx route. After crossing the Willis Avenue Bridge, runners will turn left onto East 135th Street, then right onto Alexander Avenue. They will continue along Alexander Avenue before turning left onto East 141st Street, followed by a left onto Third Avenue and a right onto East 138th Street. The route then crosses the Madison Avenue Bridge back into Manhattan.

Runners and spectators can view and download the latest course map through the New York Road Runners official course page . The page also provides an interactive Google Map showing course locations and race-day amenities.

NYRR records official finishers through 10:00 p.m. ET.

Several major bridges, avenues and local streets will close to accommodate runners, spectators, medical personnel and race operations.

Some restrictions also begin on Saturday, October 31 because of the Abbott Dash to the Finish Line 5K and marathon preparations.

City officials urge anyone trying to attend the race or just get around the city to take public transit.

articles.title: Double Olympic medallist PV Sindhu enters her second final in two weeks after defeating compatriot Anmol Kharb at Hylo Open badminton tournament
articles.summary: Double Olympic medallist PV Sindhu continued her impressive form by reaching the final of the Hylo Open Super 500 badminton tournament on Saturday.
articles.body: Double Olympic medallist PV Sindhu continued her impressive form by reaching the final of the Hylo Open Super 500 badminton tournament on Saturday.The Indian shuttler defeated compatriot Anmol Kharb in straight games, winning 21-13, 21-16 in just 32 minutes in the women's semifinal.This marks Sindhu's second consecutive final appearance in as many weeks. She had finished as the runner-up at the French Open last week and will now look to go one step further in Germany.The 31-year-old Sindhu used her attacking shots, accurate net play and experience to keep the 19-year-old Anmol under pressure. Although Anmol briefly took the lead in both games, she struggled to maintain consistency against her senior opponent.Sindhu controlled most of the opening game and took it 21-13 after building a comfortable lead. The second game was more competitive, with Anmol briefly moving ahead 15-13. However, Sindhu quickly fought back to level the score at 15-15 before taking control and sealing the match 21-16.Anmol, currently ranked 53rd in the world, was playing in only her second Super 500 semifinal. She had previously reached the last four of the Arctic Open last year. She was also part of India's gold medal-winning team at the 2024 Asia Team Championships.Sindhu reaches another finalThis was the second meeting between Sindhu and Anmol. Sindhu had also defeated the youngster in straight games at the Syed Modi India International in 2024.With this victory, Sindhu has reached her second final in two weeks and will hope to add another title to her impressive career.Meanwhile, another Indian shuttler, Lakshya Sen, is scheduled to face France's Toma Junior Popov later on Saturday.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Dakar Youth Olympics: Who gets to hold the flame?
articles.summary: Senegal makes history by becoming the first African country to host an Olympic event.
articles.body:
Dakar, Senegal – Senegal’s teenage volleyball players were training, giving everything they had. And I could see it in their eyes: the flame, that desire to win.

I was with my daughter and could see the effect it had on her: watching another girl her age play for a team, for a chance at gold, for something bigger than herself.

I saw it again when my daughter helped a young boxer wrap her hands, before the fighter slipped on her gloves and threw a punch few adults could withstand, and when she helped a rowing captain into the water.

There is an ease with which teenagers find one another, a friendliness adults seem to have forgotten.

And so the 2026 Youth Olympic Games opening on the world’s youngest continent on Saturday feels fitting, particularly in this sports-crazy city I call home.

Looking around Dakar, almost everyone looks like an athlete.

Surfers paddle out at dawn. Children play basketball and football in the streets. Teenagers wrestle on beaches; others swim towards Ngor Island at breakneck speed. Construction workers, after a day’s labour, gather not in pubs or bars, but on the beach – to train, laugh and listen to music.

Sport is a way of life, but also a reason to be together.

For many in Dakar, visas and money make travel beyond their borders difficult. This time the world has come to them.

The Games were supposed to take place in 2022. Then came COVID-19, and Senegal’s then-president, Macky Sall, asked for more time to prepare . The Olympics would have to wait four years.

In an interview with Al Jazeera, Kirsty Coventry, the Zimbabwean former swimmer and Olympic gold medallist who now leads the International Olympic Committee, described it as a chance for Dakar, Senegal and Africa “to actually show what we’re capable of” – not merely tell the world.

Senegal, meanwhile, is facing political and financial turmoil .

Billions of dollars of previously undisclosed debt have brought repeated credit downgrades, and the government is negotiating with creditors and the International Monetary Fund.

In a country where money is scarce, the question of what it costs to welcome the world cannot be separated from what the Games will leave behind.

Dakar can feel half built, its concrete exposed, its roads unfinished. Yet the city has done what it can with what it has. Christmas lights have become Olympic rings; and empty water bottles painted in the colours of visiting nations line roads leading towards refurbished venues.

I asked Coventry whether a country had to be wealthy to host an Olympic event.

“No,” she replied. The movement, she explained, needed to make the Games less complex and more affordable, using existing venues rather than demanding new ones.

Despite Senegal’s debt and political turmoil, the land of teranga, of hospitality, is ready to welcome some 2,700 athletes and their parents, coaches and supporters. Some have never been to Africa. Expectations are being tested, sometimes quietly, in encounters no opening ceremony could arrange.

The Olympic flame , meanwhile, has passed from hand to hand. Khaby Lame, the TikTok star known for making millions laugh without speaking, carried it through Dakar. Then came Omar Sy, the actor who plays a thief in Lupin, running through his Senegalese father’s homeland, not like a thief but like a man who belonged, carrying something he was meant to give away.

Online, the jokes from locals came quickly: Would the electricity company embarrass Senegal with a power cut? Why are some business leaders so eager to hold the flame at Games meant for teenagers? Why do adults always want to hog the limelight…?

And increasingly, the Games are unfolding on mobile phones. Athletes film themselves opening their kit, boarding planes, arriving in Dakar, sharing what they find.

Australia has sent 41 teenagers on a journey of more than 24 hours. Britain’s young coastal rowers are preparing to race. Six refugee athletes, based in Africa, are competing under a flag of their own. These teenagers are their own broadcasters, their own brands.

Already, politics has slipped into the Games. Ukraine’s public broadcaster has refused to show the ceremonies because Russian and Belarusian teenagers will compete under their national flags.

The values Coventry spoke of – friendship, excellence, respect and the ideal of neutrality – are harder for adults to practise than to pronounce.

But politics has long accompanied the Games.

Jesse Owens won four gold medals in Hitler’s Berlin in 1936, the year the modern torch relay began. In 1968, Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised black-gloved fists on the podium in Mexico City, protesting racial injustice and poverty.

Pierre de Coubertin, the French founder of the modern Olympic movement, once spoke of sport’s “conquest” of Africa. In Paris in 1900, Haitian-born rugby player Constantin Henriquez became the first known Black Olympic gold medallist.

It took more than a hundred years for the flame to come to Africa.

In 2004, Egyptian judoka Mohamed Rashwan carried the flame through Cairo on its first visit to the continent.

But competitive sport did not begin in Greece. Ancient Egyptian tomb paintings show wrestlers locked together centuries before the first recorded Games at Olympia. And Dakar had hosted its own Friendship Games in 1963, helping lay the groundwork for the All-Africa Games.

This is more than a sporting moment, especially for teenagers. Across the world, young people are protesting, hoping to be heard, to be seen, not to be ignored.

Coventry told me they want “genuine and authentic engagement”, not just the appearance of being heard. I thought of the girls training, and how little it took for my daughter to feel part of their world.

When these Games end, the visitors will go. The cauldron will go dark. Dakar will still be unfinished.

The torch will leave. But the flame I saw in those teenagers, and in my daughter, will remain.

articles.title: Team USA standout Jack Alexy sets 100m freestyle world record at USA Swimming Short Course Trials
articles.summary: Jack Alexy clocked 44.64 seconds in the 100 freestyle at the USA Swimming Short Course Trials, shattering the previous world record of 44.84.
articles.body: There’s a new world record holder in the men’s 100 freestyle, as Jack Alexy, who represented the United States in the 2024 Paris Olympics, smashed the accolade on Saturday. Alexy, racing for the California Golden Bears in the 2026 USA Swimming Short Course World Championship Trials in Westmont, Illinois, came down the final stretch in the pool with a chance to break the previous 44.84-second record. Reaching for the wall, Alexy got his hand on it at 44.64. As he looked up at the final time, he slapped the water in elation, understanding that he is in the record books now. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Alexy has flirted with the world record in the past, winning his first individual gold medal in the men’s 100-meter free final at the World Aquatics Swimming Championships in Budapest in December 2024. He had an official time of 45.38 seconds. AMERICAN JACK ALEXY WINS FIRST INDIVIDUAL GOLD MEDAL IN MEN’S 100M FREE FINAL AT WORLD SWIMMING CHAMPIONSHIPS Alexy’s Team USA teammate from Paris, Chris Guiliano, swimming for the University of Notre Dame, finished second in this race with a final time of 45.22. And another Olympian, Caeleb Dressel, came in third at 45.65. Alexy took home his first gold medal in the 4x100-meter freestyle at the Paris Olympics in 2024. Then, he broke the American and world championship record with a lead-off time of 45.05 seconds in Hungary months later. Guiliano was also on that relay squad. This world record comes four weeks after Russia’s Egor Kornev equaled the world record in the short-course version of the 100-meter freestyle during the World Cup competition. "That felt pretty good," Alexy said after his race, per Swimming World Magazine. "The goal was to qualify for the 50 and 100 individually. I was pretty confident I could get that done after this morning. "I tried to ride the adrenaline of the crowd. Any time I have the opportunity to race against a U.S. field like that at a selection meet, it is more nerve-wracking, which is a good thing. It is a good thing to have that pressure because that is what we will be facing." articles.title: Kate Douglass cierra el octubre de los récords con otro más en 100 libre
articles.standfirst: Se han batido once plusmarcas en un mes para recordar en piscina corta
articles.summary: Se han batido once plusmarcas en un mes para recordar en piscina corta
articles.body: Exprimiéndolo hasta el último día, la natación mundial ha rejuvenecido en octubre. Once plusmarcas mundiales han modernizado la tabla de los récords, más de la mitad logradas en los Campeonatos estadounidenses de selección. Incluso, en este periodo, se igualaron otras dos más. "Además de que se están acercando a los límites", explica Santi Veiga, el seleccionador español. "una de las razones es que los estadounidenses nadan en sus universidades en piscinas de 25 yardas, no 25 metros, y sólo se adentran en estas medidas cuando llegan los Mundiales, como este año en Pekín. Si estuviesen nadando todo el día en ellas, tal como dominan el nado subacuático, se bajarian más las marcas". Especialmente cobran sentido las palabras de Veiga en el sector femenino donde Kate Douglass, la mejor velocista del mundo y otro producto más de la Universidad de Virginia, devoró el de 100 libre. Lo rebajó hasta 49.64, 29 centésimas menos que el registro que ella había marcado el año pasado cuando se convirtió en la primera mujer en bajar de 50 segundos. Su nado fue rapidísimo en el inicio -pasó el 50 en 23.52 (41 centésimas mejor que la referencia anterior)- y mantuvo un ritmo frenético hasta el final. Douglass, que posee también la plusmarca mundial de 50 libre en piscina olímpica, ha ganado cuatro pruebas en los Trials celebrados en Westmont, Illinois. Ganó los 50 igualando el récord de Gretchen Walsh y ha vencido en los 200 brazas y los 200 estilos. Gretchen, su compañera de entrenamientos, fue segunda el sábado con 50.61, casi un segundo más lenta. La noche pudo ser redonda para las 'Lady Cavaliers', pero Claire Curzan se quedó a 32 centésimas del récord del mundo de 200 espalda que posee Kaylee McKeown. Nadó en 1:57.65. El viernes había batido el de 100 espalda. De la tabla individual femenina, las estadounidenses poseen 11 de las 18 plusmarcas. Douglass aparece en cuatro de ellas. La profundidad de armario de la natación estadounidense les permitirá atender al mismo tiempo a los Mundiales de corta de Pekín y el US Open de piscina de 50 metros que se celebra en las mismas fechas (1 al 6 de diciembre), competición en la que estarán, por ejemplo, Katie Ledecky, Torri Huske y Ryan Murphy. Douglass, las hermanas Walsh y Caeleb Dressel liderarán la tropa en la capital china. También estará Ilya Kharun, el ucraniano hijo de acróbatas del Circo del Soleil, que ha cambiado Canadá -con la que consiguió dos bronces en los Juegos Olímpicos de París- por Estados Unidos.

articles.title: Maratón de Nueva York 2026: horario, dónde ver hoy en TV y canal de la carrera
articles.standfirst: La emblemática prueba estadounidense reúne a la élite y a miles de corredores populares en un recorrido por los cinco distritos de Nueva York
articles.summary: La emblemática prueba estadounidense reúne a la élite y a miles de corredores populares en un recorrido por los cinco distritos de Nueva York
articles.body: El Maratón de Nueva York celebra hoy domingo 1 de noviembre una nueva edición de una de las carreras más populares y reconocibles del calendario internacional. Atletas de élite y corredores aficionados volverán a recorrer las calles de la Gran Manzana en una jornada que convierte a la ciudad estadounidense en el epicentro mundial del atletismo. La prueba arranca en Staten Island y conduce a los participantes por los cinco distritos de la ciudad: Brooklyn, Queens, Manhattan, El Bronx y nuevamente Manhattan. La meta está situada en Central Park, escenario habitual de la llegada después de los 42,195 kilómetros reglamentarios. Entre los puntos más característicos del recorrido aparecen el puente Verrazzano-Narrows, el Queensboro Bridge y la entrada definitiva en Central Park. La exigencia de sus puentes y desniveles hace que no sea uno de los circuitos más rápidos, pero su ambiente y su relevancia internacional lo convierten en una de las grandes citas de cada temporada. El Maratón de Nueva York forma parte del circuito de grandes maratones internacionales junto con las pruebas de Boston, Londres, Berlín, Chicago y Tokio. La retransmisión en España del Maratón de Nueva York comienza hoy domingo 1 de noviembre a las 14:30 horas, según el horario peninsular español. La prueba dispone de diferentes salidas para las categorías de silla de ruedas, atletas profesionales y las sucesivas oleadas de corredores populares. Por ese motivo, la hora de conexión televisiva no debe interpretarse necesariamente como el inicio de todas las categorías. El Maratón de Nueva York podrá verse en directo y en abierto a través de Teledeporte. La programación deportiva de MARCA sitúa la conexión con la carrera a partir de las 14:30 horas. Toda la actualidad de la carrera podrá consultarse igualmente en MARCA.com, con los resultados, las clasificaciones y la información de los principales protagonistas al término de la prueba.

articles.title: Heidi Klum's Halloween costume revealed as Traitors' Maya Jama dresses as Mo Farah
articles.summary: Celebrities have been embracing the scariest day of the year by dressing up as sport stars, dismembered limbs and unsold concert tickets.
articles.body:
Supermodel and TV host Heidi Klum confirmed her position as the queen of Halloween by transforming into a giant, bloodied and severed hand for her annual costume party in New York.

Klum, 53, was completely unrecognisable arriving at her event in what she described as her own chopped-off "left hand".

This year marks the 25th anniversary of Klum's party, which brings celebrities across the globe together dressed in their wild, weird and wonderful costumes.

And the revelry didn't stop there, with celebrities such as Maya Jama wowing attendees at her own Halloween party in London dressed as four-time Olympic champion Sir Mo Farah.

"It took a lot of hands putting this hand together," Klum told reporters as she posed for pictures on the red carpet. "I think about 10 or 20 hands."

Explaining the inspiration for the idea, she said: "I looked at my hand and I thought 'Hey, I think that I can fit my body inside of this somehow.'

"I always try to come up with something unusual and I don't think I've seen an actual person walking around like a hand. I thought that was something new and different."

Klum is never one to shy away from dressing up on the scariest day of the year, with previous looks including a worm, Medusa and the ogre Princess Fiona from the Shrek films.

Other attendees at Klum's party this year included actors Neil Patrick Harris and David Burtka, who surprised attendees by dressing as the twins from the horror film The Shining.

Pop star Jade Thirlwall also attended the party in New York dressed as a stone statue of an angel, while Severance and Spider-Man actor Tramell Tillman turned up with intricate face makeup and prosthetics.

Meanwhile in London, broadcaster Maya Jama hosted her annual Halloween Party dressed as Sir Mo Farah.

Jama told Elle UK magazine she wanted to dress as the "bald headed icon" to honour the Olympian, adding that she has wanted to dress up as a man for years for Halloween.

"[Sir Mo] loved the idea," she explained.

"He's actually sent me all of his real life Olympic outfits, his real, actual medals he won for the Olympics.

articles.title: Ciara Mageean: European champion and Olympian dies aged 34
articles.summary: Ciara Mageean, who won a European title and twice represented Ireland at the Olympics, dies aged 34.
articles.body:
Former European champion and two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean has died at the age of 34.

Mageean, from Portaferry in Northern Ireland, was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025.

She represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics, but was forced to withdraw from the 2024 Paris Games because of an Achilles injury.

Earlier in 2024, Mageean had clinched the first major title of her career when she took 1500m gold at the European Championships in Rome.

Prior to that she had also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning 1500m silver at Birmingham 2022.

A statement posted on her social media on Sunday said: "At 6.30am this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones.

"A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed.

"Ar dheis Dé go raibh a hanam (may her soul rest in peace)."

In a statement on social media, Athletics Ireland said: "We are heartbroken. An inspiration to so many, Ciara will be remembered for her courage, kindness and incredible spirit.

"Our deepest sympathies are with her family, friends and loved ones at this difficult time. Rest in peace, Ciara."

In October, Mageean wed her long-term partner Thomas Moran in a small civil ceremony in Belfast.

A talented athlete from a young age, Mageean played camogie for Portaferry GAC, but her dream of representing Ireland at the Olympics led her to pursue a career in athletics.

Her running prowess was clear during an impressive junior career that yielded 1500m silvers at the 2010 World Junior Championships and 2011 European Junior Championships. She also reached the 2010 Commonwealth Games 1500m final as an 18-year-old.

However, Mageean's early progress in the senior ranks was hampered by a serious ankle injury, which ended her hopes of making her Olympic debut at London 2012.

Having had surgery in 2013, Mageean won the Irish 1500m title on her return in July 2014.

In 2016, she claimed 1500m bronze at the European Championships in Amsterdam, but her Olympic debut ended in disappointment as she exited the 1500m competition at the semi-final stage.

In late 2017, Mageean left her Dublin base to join Steve Vernon's Team New Balance in Manchester after parting ways with coach Jerry Kiernan.

And while she endured some disappointing results following the move, Mageean claimed a European Indoor bronze medal in March 2019 before clocking two minutes 31.06 seconds to take 3.6 seconds off Sonia O'Sullivan's 27-year-old Irish 1,000m record at the 2020 Diamond League Monaco meet.

Mageean endured more Olympic heartache at the delayed Tokyo Games in 2021, when a calf injury disrupted her preparations as she exited from the heats.

However, she enjoyed a successful 2022 campaign under the guidance of former Great Britain Olympian Helen Clitheroe, winning 1500m European and Commonwealth silver behind Laura Muir.

Two weeks after the Euros, Mageean beat Muir and a world-class field to seal a stunning 1500m victory at Diamond League Brussels. Her time of 3:56.63 took 2.22 seconds off O'Sullivan's Irish record and marked her first sub four-minute run.

In 2023, Mageean narrowly missed out on a World Championship medal as she finished fourth in a high-class final in Budapest.

However, after taking over two seconds off O'Sullivan's Irish mile record in July, Mageean was named the 2023 BBC Northern Ireland Sports Personality of the Year.

After a string of near-misses at championship level, Mageean secured the biggest win of her career at the 2024 European Championships in Rome.

In a gripping final, Mageean found herself boxed in behind Great Britain duo Georgia Bell and Jemma Reekie, but managed to dart through a gap and power down the straight to victory in 4:04.66.

An ecstatic Mageean, who won admirers for her honest and emotional post-race interviews down the years, said "words can't even come close" to describing how she felt after sealing the first major title of her career.

After Mageean's jubilation in Rome, injury again interrupted her Olympic bid as an Achilles injury forced her to withdraw on the eve of her heat in Paris.

Earlier this year, Mageean said she was "continuing to find the joy in everyday" as she thanked people for their support following her diagnosis.

Speaking to the BBC in June, she said she was "grateful" for having a career "that many others didn't get to have".

articles.body:
Irish middle-distance runner Ciara Mageean, who won European gold and competed at two Olympic Games, has died aged 34, her family has announced.

“At 6:30am this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones,” said a statement posted on the athlete’s Instagram account on Sunday.

Mageean’s death comes just weeks after she married her long-term boyfriend in Belfast.

She had been receiving treatment for bowel cancer, revealing her diagnosis in July 2025 and subsequently disclosing that the disease was at an advanced stage.

Originally from Portaferry in County Down, Northern Ireland, Mageean established herself as one of the island of Ireland’s leading middle-distance runners, setting several records in both Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.

She represented the republic at the 2016 Rio Olympics, at the Tokyo Games held in 2021, and in her greatest sporting achievement – in 2024 when, she claimed the 1,500 metres title at the European Athletics Championships in Rome.

But an Achilles tendon injury prevented her from competing at the Paris Olympics that year.

Mageean remained remarkably positive throughout her period of illness, saying she was “continuing to find the joy in everyday” as she thanked people for their support following her diagnosis.

Speaking to the BBC in June, she said she was “grateful” for having a career “that many others didn’t get to have”.

Tributes poured in for Mageean, who also won European bronze and silver in the 1,500m (in 2016 and 2022, respectively) and finished second in the event at the 2022 Commonwealth Games, where she represented Northern Ireland.

“The country has lost a hero,” the Olympic Federation of Ireland said in a statement.

“Beyond the medals, records and sporting accolades, Ciara will be remembered for her warmth, courage and tremendous strength of character,” said Northern Ireland’s First Minister Michelle O’Neill.

The Republic of Ireland’s prime minister, Taoiseach Micheal Martin, said he was “deeply saddened” by Mageean’s “untimely passing”.

articles.title: Ciara Mageean: Tributes to 'inspirational' Olympic athlete after death at 34
articles.summary: Sporting, political and media figures pay tribute to former European champion and Olympian Ciara Mageean following her death at 34.
articles.body:
Tributes have been paid to former European champion and two-time Olympic runner Ciara Mageean, who has died at the age of 34.

Mageean, from Portaferry in County Down, was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025.

She died on Sunday morning, surrounded by her loved ones, a statement posted on her social media accounts said.

"A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed," it said.

Mageean's death comes less than three weeks after her marriage to her long-term partner Thomas Moran .

The athlete represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics and won gold in the 1500m at the European Athletics Championships in Rome in 2024.

She also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning silver in Birmingham in 2022.

Olympic legend Lady Mary Peters said Mageean was a "wonderful lady" who was "gracious, beautiful, talented and inspirational to the next generation".

"We knew she was very ill and we knew that it was inevitable but we didn't expect it so soon," said the 1972 Olympic pentathlon gold medallist.

Lady Mary's charity the Mary Peters Trust, which supports Northern Ireland athletes, had helped Mageean in her athletics career.

"My charity supported her for as long as we could because she was so talented and we recognised that in her," said Last Mary.

She said that Mageean had continued to inspire young athletes even while undergoing treatment for cancer and would be "sorely missed in the world of sport".

Sean Young, the secretary of Portaferry Gaelic Athletic Club, where Mageean played camogie in her younger years, said its members were in "disbelief and shock" at her death.

He said Mageean had been a "fierce competitor" who began her sporting journey at the club before pursuing athletics.

"Outside the sporting arena she is the most inspirational, humble person we have ever had within our club," he said.

Obituary: Gifted athlete whose wit and smile left lasting impression

Down Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) said it was "honoured and privileged" to call Mageean one of its own, describing her as someone who never forgot her roots.

"She touched the lives of so many people and she helped change the lives of so many," it said.

"In her battle with illness she showed us courage, positivity and the value of life."

Her former school, Assumption Grammar in Ballynahinch, County Down, said it was "deeply saddened and heartbroken" by the death of its "cherished past pupil".

"Ciara's kindness, strength, faith and unwavering determination were an inspiration to us all," it said.

"She touched countless lives with her warmth, humility and generosity of spirit."

Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill described Mageean as "a champion in every sense of the word and a role model for all athletes".

"She represented her country with pride and helped put Irish athletics on the map," said O'Neill.

She said Mageean had faced her cancer diagnosis with the same "bravery and determination" she had shown throughout her sporting career.

"Ciara's legacy will live on and she will continue to be an inspiration to many."

Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said people across Northern Ireland had been "deeply proud and inspired" by the athlete.

She described Mageean as an "outstanding athlete and ambassador for her sport" who had spoken with honesty and bravery about her health battles.

Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin said he was "deeply saddened" by her untimely death and extended his sympathies to her husband, family and friends.

Tánaiste (Irish Deputy Prime Minister) Simon Harris said Mageean had inspired people both through her achievements on the track and her openness about her illness.

"She gave so many others strength and hope," he said.

World Athletics described her as "an inspiration to many, on and off the track", highlighting her historic European gold medal in Rome in 2024.

Athletics Ireland, the country's governing body for the sport, said Mageean was "much-loved and inspirational".

"Her courage, warmth and spirit will leave a lasting legacy," the organisation said.

Conal Heatley, the chief executive of Commonwealth Games Northern Ireland, described Mageean as "one of the best of us".

He told BBC News NI she had carried herself with "incredible dignity" throughout her illness and was a "fantastic figure for the island of Ireland".

The Camogie Association also paid tribute to Mageean, with its president Brian Molloy describing her as a great friend of the sport, both as a player and a supporter.

"In her all-too-short life, Ciara touched the hearts of so many," he said.

"Her self-belief and commitment to her craft will always be inspirational and she will be fondly remembered by all who had the privilege of knowing her."

Mageean was named the 2023 BBC Northern Ireland Sports Personality of the Year after an impressive year, in which she broke national records and was fourth in a competitive World Championships final.

BBC Sport NI broadcaster Thomas Niblock, who interviewed Mageean in July for The GAA Social podcast , described her as a "one off".

"A light has gone out in the world. Authentic, talented, decent. Her kindness and wonderful personality was a joy to watch and see," he wrote on social media.

Niblock recalled how Mageean had received disappointing news the day before their interview but had insisted on going ahead with the recording.

"It's 90 minutes Oisin and myself will always treasure. She was the best of us," he said.

He also paid tribute to her husband and the wider Portaferry community.

"I've never met a person who met Ciara, who didn't love her," he added.

Patrick Kielty, who said it was a "privilege" to interview Mageean on Irish national broadcaster RTÉ's The Late Late Show, said "she wasn't just a champion on the track".

"She was a champion of others who showed us all how to live."

articles.title: Ciara Mageean obituary: Gifted athlete whose wit and smile left lasting impression
articles.summary: The class and grace with which Ciara Mageean carried herself on and off the athletics track leaves a lasting impression, writes BBC Sport NI's Nigel Ringland.
articles.body:
Two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean has died at the age of 34 . BBC Sport NI's Nigel Ringland, who covered her entire career, shares his memories.

Ciara Mageean was simply one of those people you never forgot if you were lucky enough to have known her.

She will be remembered as one of Ireland's greatest athletes, but to those closest to her, she was a loving daughter and sister and just recently became a loving wife to Thomas.

I first met her at the start of 2009 at a pre-event press conference at the Odyssey Arena for the Irish National Indoor Championships.

She was already thought of in high circles as a talent for the future although she had only recently decided to focus on athletics instead of her beloved camogie.

Facing the media can be daunting for 16-year-olds, but Ciara gave a mature interview.

Even then, you could tell she was special.

Tributes paid to 'inspirational' Ciara Mageean after death at 34

The following year she represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games in Delhi, her first major senior championships.

Going into the last lap of the 1500m final, she was in last place. To be honest, she could have jogged around and no-one would have been critical of her. After all, making the final was quite the achievement.

But that wasn’t in Ciara's DNA. She battled all the way to the line to finish 10th.

That resilience and determination to fight were qualities she would show throughout her athletics career and in life itself.

Her career was a rollercoaster ride and her most memorable moments came later on.

She won European bronze in 2016, but I'd never seen her happier than she was after clinching silver at the Commonwealth Games in 2022. She followed that up with a silver at the European Championships and a first win in the Diamond League.

The following year she was fourth in the World Championships and smashing Irish records almost every time she ran.

Then came her most memorable race. The 1500m final at the 2024 European Championships in Rome.

Once again her determination not to be beaten was shown in the closing one 100 metres and she darted past Great Britain's Georgia Bell and Jemma Reekie to win gold .

It was a race that will live long in the hearts of Irish athletics fans and a moment in time that is more poignant today.

It was her moment that she shared with us all.

The stars never aligned for her at the Olympic Games. She ran in two - Rio 2016 and Tokyo 2021 - but was never at her best and even when she was two years ago, a last-minute injury stopped her competing in Paris.

She was all set to try again for Los Angeles in 2028, which was to be the swansong of her career.

That was before the devastating cancer diagnosis in May 2025.

Even then Ciara decided to share her news publicly. It was those qualities again of resilience and determination to fight and in doing so provide inspiration to those who would find themselves in a similar situation.

That was who she was, in athletics and in life - an inspiration to others

I have many memories of Ciara including surprising her at home in Portaferry with the BBC Sport Northern Ireland Personality of the Year in 2023.

Filming in Portaferry was always fun because her mum, Catherine, would always lay out a welcoming spread of scones and cake and tea.

It's Catherine and Ciara's dad Chris, her husband Thomas and family that are in my thoughts today.

When I last spoke to Ciara, her relentless positivity remained undimmed.

Her infectious personality, quick wit, and smile left a lasting impression and her achievements on the track will serve as inspiration to others to never lose hope in the pursuit of dreams.

articles.body: India continued their dominant run in the Asian Champions Trophy 2026, but not before being pushed by a spirited Malaysia side in a contest that tested their composure and attacking depth. Harmanpreet Singh rose to the occasion with a hat-trick, while Sukhjeet Singh produced a stunning field goal as the hosts secured a 4-2 victory at the Olympian Surjit Singh Hockey Stadium in Jalandhar on Sunday.The win marked India's fourth consecutive victory in the tournament, keeping their unbeaten record intact and strengthening their position heading into the final group-stage fixture against South Korea.India made a bright start and took the lead in the third minute through captain Harmanpreet, who converted a penalty corner with a powerful drag-flick. The hosts looked to build on the early advantage, but Malaysia gradually found their footing and began creating opportunities.India goalkeeper Krishan Pathak, who replaced Suraj Karkera in the second quarter, made two important saves from Malaysian penalty corners to preserve the lead. However, Malaysia eventually found the equaliser in the 25th minute. Akhimullah Anuar finished off a move involving Faiz Jali and Faisal Saari, poking the ball past Pathak to make it 1-1.India had opportunities to regain the lead before half-time, with Harmanpreet striking the crossbar from a penalty corner. Mandeep Singh also missed a close-range chance as the teams went into the break level.Harmanpreet, Sukhjeet take charge after the breakIndia returned with greater urgency in the third quarter and regained the lead in the 33rd minute. Harmanpreet once again stepped up from a penalty corner, sending a low drag-flick into the bottom corner to make it 2-1.Malaysia's task became tougher when Faiz Jali received a 10-minute yellow card in the 38th minute for a challenge on Mandeep. articles.title: Almgren, en su debut, y Chepkirui reinan en el maratón de Nueva York
articles.standfirst: El sueco cierra un año de ensueño tras el oro europeo y el oro mundial de medio maratón, mientras que la keniata repite título en la prueba de la Gran Manzana
articles.summary: El sueco cierra un año de ensueño tras el oro europeo y el oro mundial de medio maratón, mientras que la keniata repite título en la prueba de la Gran Manzana
articles.body: Nueva York nunca defrauda. Un debutante en la distancia, el sueco Andreas Almgren, y la ganadora de 2024, Sheila Chepkirui, se proclamaron campeones del maratón de la Gran Manzana, en el 50 aniversario del recorrido de la prueba por los cinco distritos de la ciudad. Fueron dos carreras apasionantes en los metros finales, con duelos espectaculares y sendas victorias que se cimentaron en el último kilómetro: Almgren superó con mucha solvencia a Crippa, mientras que Chepkirui batió a Obiri, que pagó el esfuerzo final. Antes de eso, ambas pruebas transcurrieron con un guion similar, con un nutrido grupo de favoritos que marchó sin cambios en los primeros kilómetros. En categoría masculina, Benson Kipruto, ganador el pasado año, lideró la prueba, junto a Conner Mantz, plusmarquista estadounidense de la distancia, o el sueco Andreas Almgren, campeón del mundo de medio maratón y de Europa de 10.000. Fue en el kilómetro 15 cuando Deresa Geleta intentó lanzar un primer ataque, pero el cambio fue repelido por el resto del grupo, donde también figuraban el italiano Crippa o el japonés Suzuki. Lo intentó también el local Talbi, que cambió su frecuencia de zancada antes del medio maratón para sacar unos metros al grupo. Crippa y Kiprop se fueron a por el estadounidense (1.04:01 al paso por el medio maratón), que volvió a acelerar para intentar romper la carrera. No lo logró y el desenlace, con aún casi 20 atletas en el grupo de cabeza -algo inusual-, se retrasó hasta los kilómetros finales. Se sucedieron los cambios de ritmo antes del kilómetro 40 y salieron victoriosos de ellos Crippa, Kipruto y Almgren, que se lanzaron a por el triunfo. El keniata, sin embargo, empezó a pagar el ritmo de cabeza, en el que el sueco y el italiano, muy fuertes, se jugaron la victoria. Los dos atletas, muy experimentados en pista, aceleraron en los últimos metros, pero Almgren, más solvente, se fue solo hasta el final. El sueco, que ya protagonizó sendas exhibiciones en los 10.000 del pasado Europeo y en el Mundial de medio maratón, protagonizó un final histórico para ganar en Nueva York en su debut (2.06:01) y erigirse en el primer atleta no nacido en África en llevarse un 'major' ocho años después. Crippa, otro europeo, fue segundo, con 2.06:14, mientras que Mofolo, de Lesotho, completó el podio, con 2.06:26. El grupo de favoritas fue compacto desde el inicio. En los primeros 20 kilómetros, apenas hubo ataques, por lo que Obiri, que defendía el triunfo del pasado año, así como Chepkirui, ganadora en 2024, o Edna Kiplagat continuaron en cabeza, junto al resto de sus principales rivales. En el kilómetro 20, un desordenado avituallamiento, en el que Kelati tuvo que frenar y volver unos pasos atrás para coger el bote, perturbó por momento la homogeneidad del grupo, en el que hubo atletas que tuvieron que esforzarse para seguir a Obiri y compañía, entre las que también figuraban las locales McClain o Ellwood. Tras el medio maratón, que pasaron en 1.13:52, Obiri incrementó el ritmo y obligó al resto a responder. A medida que transcurrían los kilómetros, el grupo perdió efectivos, como Wood o Hagans, y en el kilómetro 36 se fueron arriba Chepkirui y Obiri, que se jugaron el triunfo final en un pulso entre ambas. Chepkirui hizo todo el trabajo en los kilómetros finales, intentó Obiri superarla en varias ocasiones, incluso los últimos metros, pero no lo logró, por lo que la keniata se impuso en 2.24:36, para repetir triunfo en Nueva York. Tal fue el esfuerzo de Obiri al final, que fue superada por la estadounidense McClain casi en línea de meta (2.24:42). La ganadora del pasado año completó el podio, con 2.24:43.

articles.title: Martín Fiz cierra el círculo en Nueva York con su último maratón, el nº 42
articles.standfirst: El campeón de Europa y del mundo disputó en la Gran Manzana su última prueba competitiva en la distancia junto a su hijo y su mujer y terminó en 3.01:13
articles.summary: El campeón de Europa y del mundo disputó en la Gran Manzana su última prueba competitiva en la distancia junto a su hijo y su mujer y terminó en 3.01:13
articles.body: La vida de Marín Fiz no se entiende sin el maratón. En los 42.195 kilómetros, sobre el asfalto, el atleta (Vitoria, 1963) encontró su 'leitmotiv', la prueba que le permitió alcanzar los mayores logros de su carrera deportiva, entre ellos el oro mundial en Goteborg en 1995 y el título europeo en Helsinki en 1994. Desde su primer maratón, allá por 1993, Martín Fiz ha disputado esta distancia en 41 ocasiones y este domingo, en un escenario único como Nueva York, ha corrido su último maratón competitivo, el número 42. Lo ha hecho de la manera más especial posible, junto a su mujer Ana y su hijo Álex, en el que era su debut en la distancia. Así, en la ciudad de los rascacielos, Fiz ha cerrado el círculo a una carrera deportiva de ensueño, que tuvo en el oro mundial y el título europeo sus mayores conquistas. Pero no son los únicos. El vitoriano atesora también un subcampeonato mundial (Atenas, 1997) y dos diplomas olímpicos, tras su cuarto puesto en Atlanta'96 y el sexto en Sidney 2000. Este palmarés le llevó a ser reconocido con el premio Príncipe de Asturias de los Deportes en 1997 junto al equipo español de maratón. Tras cerrar su etapa en la élite, Fiz continuó compitiendo... y siguió ganando. En abril de 2018 culminó en Londres su reto de ganar los llamados seis 'Majors' (los mejores maratones del mundo) dentro de su categoría, mayores de 55 años. Se convirtió así en el primer atleta en sumar victorias en los seis grandes, tras ganar Nueva York (2015), Tokio, Boston y Berlín (2016) y Chicago (2017), además de Londres. Después, en 2025, también completó las SuperHalfs, el circuito internacional de carreras de medio maratón: Lisboa (Portugal), Copenhague (Dinamarca), Cardiff (Gales), Praga (República Checa), Berlín (Alemania) y Valencia, en las que también se impuso en su categoría. Ahora, después de 300.000 kilómetros en sus piernas según sus cálculos, Martín acaba Nueva York en 3.01:13, junto a su familia, en la despedida más especial. "Estoy ilusionado, no apenado", reconocía a la salida.

articles.title: New York Marathon: Andreas Almgren wins men's race on his marathon debut
articles.summary: Andreas Almgren continues his remarkable year by winning the New York Marathon on his debut over 26.2 miles.
articles.body:
Andreas Almgren continued his remarkable year by winning the New York Marathon men's race on his debut over 26.2 miles.

The 31-year-old Swede broke the European half-marathon record in September, having already won 10,000m gold at the European Athletics Championships in August.

Almgren then lived up to the anticipation surrounding his marathon debut by finishing in two hours, six minutes and one second in New York - 13 seconds in front of Italy's Yemaneberhan Crippa.

Lesotho's Kamohelo Mofolo finished a further 12 seconds back in third.

Almgren became the first European-born man in 30 years to win the race in New York, after Italy's Giacomo Leone in 1996.

"I just thought, 'I've got the legs today'," said Almgren.

"I'm about to start crying. It's better than anything I could have ever imagined."

In the women's race, Kenya's Sheila Chepkirui claimed her second New York Marathon success.

The 35-year-old finished in 2:24:36, which was six seconds ahead of American Jessica McClain, with Kenya's Hellen Obiri a further second back.

"The last mile was really tricky and I had to be patient because I knew Hellen was really strong," said Chepkirui.

"I had to really push up to the finish line."

The race marked the 50th anniversary of the marathon, which links New York's five boroughs of Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan.

articles.title: Tributes to 'inspirational' Olympian Ciara Mageean after death at 34
articles.summary: Sporting, political and media figures pay tribute to former European champion and Olympian Ciara Mageean following her death at 34.
articles.body:
Tributes have been paid to former European champion and two-time Olympic runner Ciara Mageean, who has died at the age of 34.

Mageean, from Portaferry in County Down, was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025.

She died on Sunday morning, surrounded by her loved ones, a statement posted on her social media accounts said.

"A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed," it said.

Mageean's death comes less than three weeks after her marriage to her long-term partner Thomas Moran .

The athlete represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics and won gold in the 1500m at the European Athletics Championships in Rome in 2024.

She also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning silver in Birmingham in 2022.

Olympic legend Lady Mary Peters said Mageean was a "wonderful lady" who was "gracious, beautiful, talented and inspirational to the next generation".

"We knew she was very ill and we knew that it was inevitable but we didn't expect it so soon," said the 1972 Olympic pentathlon gold medallist.

Lady Mary's charity the Mary Peters Trust, which supports Northern Ireland athletes, had helped Mageean in her athletics career.

"My charity supported her for as long as we could because she was so talented and we recognised that in her," said Last Mary.

She said that Mageean had continued to inspire young athletes even while undergoing treatment for cancer and would be "sorely missed in the world of sport".

Sean Young, the secretary of Portaferry Gaelic Athletic Club, where Mageean played camogie in her younger years, said its members were in "disbelief and shock" at her death.

He said Mageean had been a "fierce competitor" who began her sporting journey at the club before pursuing athletics.

"Outside the sporting arena she is the most inspirational, humble person we have ever had within our club," he said.

Down Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) said it was "honoured and privileged" to call Mageean one of its own, describing her as someone who never forgot her roots.

"She touched the lives of so many people and she helped change the lives of so many," it said.

"In her battle with illness she showed us courage, positivity and the value of life."

Her former school, Assumption Grammar in Ballynahinch, County Down, said it was "deeply saddened and heartbroken" by the death of its "cherished past pupil".

"Ciara's kindness, strength, faith and unwavering determination were an inspiration to us all," it said.

"She touched countless lives with her warmth, humility and generosity of spirit."

Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill described Mageean as "a champion in every sense of the word and a role model for all athletes".

"She represented her country with pride and helped put Irish athletics on the map," said O'Neill.

She said Mageean had faced her cancer diagnosis with the same "bravery and determination" she had shown throughout her sporting career.

"Ciara's legacy will live on and she will continue to be an inspiration to many."

Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said people across Northern Ireland had been "deeply proud and inspired" by the athlete.

She described Mageean as an "outstanding athlete and ambassador for her sport" who had spoken with honesty and bravery about her health battles.

Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin said he was "deeply saddened" by her untimely death and extended his sympathies to her husband, family and friends.

Tánaiste (Irish Deputy Prime Minister) Simon Harris said Mageean had inspired people both through her achievements on the track and her openness about her illness.

"She gave so many others strength and hope," he said.

World Athletics described her as "an inspiration to many, on and off the track", highlighting her historic European gold medal in Rome in 2024.

Athletics Ireland, the country's governing body for the sport, said Mageean was "much-loved and inspirational".

"Her courage, warmth and spirit will leave a lasting legacy," the organisation said.

Conal Heatley, the chief executive of Commonwealth Games Northern Ireland, described Mageean as "one of the best of us".

He told BBC News NI she had carried herself with "incredible dignity" throughout her illness and was a "fantastic figure for the island of Ireland".

The Camogie Association also paid tribute to Mageean, with its president Brian Molloy describing her as a great friend of the sport, both as a player and a supporter.

"In her all-too-short life, Ciara touched the hearts of so many," he said.

"Her self-belief and commitment to her craft will always be inspirational and she will be fondly remembered by all who had the privilege of knowing her."

Mageean was named the 2023 BBC Northern Ireland Sports Personality of the Year after an impressive year, in which she broke national records and was fourth in a competitive World Championships final.

BBC Sport NI broadcaster Thomas Niblock, who interviewed Mageean in July for The GAA Social podcast , described her as a "one off".

"A light has gone out in the world. Authentic, talented, decent. Her kindness and wonderful personality was a joy to watch and see," he wrote on social media.

Niblock recalled how Mageean had received disappointing news the day before their interview but had insisted on going ahead with the recording.

"It's 90 minutes Oisin and myself will always treasure. She was the best of us," he said.

He also paid tribute to her husband and the wider Portaferry community.

"I've never met a person who met Ciara, who didn't love her," he added.

Patrick Kielty, who said it was a "privilege" to interview Mageean on Irish national broadcaster RTÉ's The Late Late Show, said "she wasn't just a champion on the track".

"She was a champion of others who showed us all how to live."

articles.title: New York Marathon Results 2026 for Men's & Women's Top Finishers and Notable Celebrities
articles.summary: The winners of the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon in the women's and men's fields featured a familiar face as well as a newcomer.
articles.body:
The winners of the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon in the women's and men's fields featured a familiar face as well as a newcomer.

The women's race was won by Sheila Chepkirui of Kenya, who was previously the winner of the event in 2024. Meanwhile, Sweden's Andreas Almgren ended up emerging victorious in the men's race as he made his marathon debut.

Chepkirui was able to pull away from Kenya's Hellen Obiri across the final 150 meters. Obiri, a two-time New York City Marathon winner and the defending champion, was passed by Jessica McClain of the United States just before the finish line.

Almgren became the first Swede to win the New York City Marathon, as Italy's Yemaneberhan Crippa finished at No. 2.

Almgren entered Saturday's race as the reigning world champion in the half-marathon, but had never participated in a 26.2-mile course.

"I just tried to stay up at front and see what happened and see how the race developed," Almgren said after his victory, per Doug Feinberg of the Associated Press. "I didn't think it was going to be that quick of a finish, but I didn't really know anything about that. One of the reasons I choose to race New York is that you don't care about the time but just get as good a position as possible."

He posted the third-fastest time in the 50-year history of the course, which goes through all five New York City boroughs.

American Zouhair Talbi finished at No. 6 in the men's race, representing the fastest time by a U.S. runner in the event (h/t Feinberg).

As for Chepkirui, she explained how difficult it was to pull away from her countrymate and seal her victory.

"The last mile was really tricky," Chepkirui said, per ESPN. "I had to be patient because I knew Hellen was really strong, so I had to really push up to the finish line."

McClain, who edged out Obiri by one second for the No. 2 spot, became the first U.S. woman to finish in the top three since 2018.

articles.title: Senegal hosts Africa’s first Olympics
articles.summary: The head of the International Olympic Committee discusses the significance of Africa hosting the Youth Olympic Games.
articles.body:
More than 2,000 athletes from around the world are in Senegal for the Youth Olympic Games to compete in Africa’s first Olympic event.

The head of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), Kirsty Coventry, says this is a milestone, not just for Senegal but for the continent, which has the largest youth population. The games, postponed four years ago because of the COVID-19 pandemic, are being viewed as a test for Africa to see whether it can handle major international sports events.

She says this is a chance for Africa to show the world what it is capable of hosting such big events. Herself an Olympic gold medallist in swimming, Coventry tells Al Jazeera she hopes the games will empower young people and inspire them to dream big.

But as the Olympic flame burns bright in Senegal – the future of the youth games is uncertain. Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye says hosting the event is a proud moment. However, the country is facing economic challenges, and some critics say the money could have been better spent elsewhere.

Coventry says the IOC is re-evaluating its direction and examining how to reduce the costs of hosting.

articles.title: Beth Dobbin: Tom Daley and David Moyes among 360 sportspeople to sign letter to Andy Burnham
articles.summary: A total of 360 sportspeople sign a letter calling on the prime minister to meet Beth Dobbin and increase funding towards ME research.
articles.body:
More than 350 sportspeople - including Olympians Dina Asher-Smith and Tom Daley - have signed a letter to the prime minister calling on him to meet former sprinter Beth Dobbin and commit to increased funding towards ME research.

Dobbin, 32, recently revealed in an interview with BBC Sport she had been diagnosed with "life-decimating" ME (myalgic encephalomyelitis) and as a result spends more than 22 hours a day in bed.

ME is a chronic, fluctuating disease, causing symptoms such as sleep problems, issues with thinking and memory, pain, and severe persistent fatigue that does not improve with rest, and more. It has no known cure or specific treatment.

More than 400,000 people in the UK are thought to have ME, though the true figure could exceed one million, with severity ranging from people able to work or study to those requiring round-the-clock care and tube feeding.

On 21 October, Dobbin wrote to the prime minister but did not receive a response - and she has now been backed by athletes across sport.

"For many of my team-mates, I dropped off the face of the earth four years ago when I developed severe ME," she said.

"I've been taken aback and extremely touched by how many of them - and so many others in the sports world - have jumped at the chance to help by signing this letter. It means so much to me.

"I hope that, with all of them behind me, Andy Burnham is listening and will commit to doing what's needed to deliver real change for a community that has been neglected for so long."

Among the 360 sporting figures to have signed the letter are Everton manager David Moyes, his United States women's counterpart Emma Hayes, and former Chelsea and England centre-back Millie Bright. Athletes Laura Muir, Eilish McColgan and Adam Gemili are among 114 Olympians and Paralympians to have added their support.

The letter calls on Burnham to "level the playing field" for funding into ME research with that for other illnesses "to give hope to the many affected that something is being done about this life-destroying, much-ignored illness and its spiralling impact".

It says: "The disease has received extremely low levels of research funding compared to other conditions. Between 2019 to 2024, UK government research funders committed just £6.6m in funding for research into ME, compared to £79.1m for Parkinson's and £496.4m for dementia.

"Prior to this, biomedical research funding was almost non-existent. As a result of the lack of research funding, there are no approved treatments."

The Olympic sprinter now bedbound for 22 hours a day

Olympian Dobbin writes to Prime Minister over ME funding

Dobbin chose to speak out about her illness despite knowing doing the interview could trigger a brutal deterioration in her health.

ME patients often rely on off-label medication to manage a condition that can cause more than 200 symptoms, including nausea, headaches, poor cognitive function and brain fog.

A conversation, or even something as simple as a light too bright or a sound too loud, can cause a "crash" that lasts 24, 48 hours, or in the worst cases, months.

Since the interview, she has experienced several "bad days" and has only had the physical strength to take a bath once a week.

"I've not gone into like a full-blown crash as of yet which is really good but it is the nature of the illness that at any point you can just be tipped over," she said.

"It's been so much mentally and cognitively that I've had to really pull back physically, so I'm in bed even more hours of the day."

Dobbin has been overwhelmed by the reaction - the size of which she had never anticipated.

"I've had thousands and thousands of messages of support," she said.

"It's really shocked me how much it's spread worldwide. I've had messages from America, Canada, Australia, all around Europe. It really has gone massive."

Karen Hargrave, co-founder of the charity ThereForME, said: "Beth's advocacy has been extraordinary, and today's letter, with the incredible support behind it, will mean so much to so many people with ME across the UK.

"Successive governments have failed people with ME, and we hope Andy Burnham's government will finally change that. The prime minister can start by meeting Beth and closing the £15m funding gap for Sequence ME & Long Covid, a vital first step towards putting ME research funding on an equal footing with other diseases."

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson previously told BBC Sport: "Myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME) can have a devastating impact on people's lives, and we are determined to accelerate progress in understanding and treating this debilitating condition.

"That is why we are supporting cutting edge research into ME, including a first-of-its-kind programme studying genetic factors behind the condition and a clinical trial for potential new treatments.

"We have published a plan, developed with the ME community, to boost research, raise awareness and support people living with the condition and we are committed to delivering on it."

articles.title: First time since 2020, Russia's flag and national anthem return to Olympics as IOC eases restrictions
articles.summary: Russia has returned to the Olympic stage with its national flag and anthem for the first time since 2020, with 13 athletes competing at the Dakar 2026
articles.body: Russia has returned to the Olympic stage with its national flag and anthem for the first time since 2020, with 13 athletes competing at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Senegal. The return comes after six years of restrictions linked to the country's doping scandal and Ukraine war.Russian athletes had been required to compete under neutral identities at subsequent Olympic events. They were not allowed to represent their country through its flag, anthem or national symbols. However, the arrangement has changed at the Youth Olympics, which opened on Saturday, October 31.The development follows a gradual easing of restrictions by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) in 2026. In July, the IOC provisionally lifted the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee and withdrew its recommendations restricting the participation of Russian and Belarusian athletes in international competitions. Individual sports federations, however, continue to decide which athletes are eligible to compete.Ukraine has not boycotted sporting events in which Russian athletes have participated. Boycotts were once a common feature of international sport, with three successive Summer Olympics, from 1976 to 1984, affected by them. In the latter two cases, the IOC was more affected than the intended targets.Youth Olympics open in SenegalThe Youth Olympic Games opened in Senegal on Saturday, marking the first Olympic event to be held in Africa. The Games are also part of the continent's efforts to play a bigger role in international sport.Tens of thousands of spectators attended the opening ceremony at the Diamniadio Olympic Stadium, near the capital Dakar. Hundreds of drummers and dancers showcased Senegalese and African culture under the Games motto, “Africa welcomes, Dakar celebrates.”Performers dressed in yellow, black and white traditional Senegalese gowns came together to form a giant map of Africa. The ceremony also featured West African oral storytelling, concerts by Senegalese singers and the athletes' parade.Around 2,700 athletes aged 14 to 17 will compete across Dakar, nearby Diamniadio and the beach resort of Saly until November 13.Russia's 13-member contingent is competing under its national flag for the first time at an Olympic event since the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 led to its suspension.The Games will also feature the first refugee team at a Youth Olympics. The six athletes, based in Kenya and Uganda, will compete in track and field, judo and taekwondo.Athletes will compete for medals across 153 events in 25 sports. Singapore hosted the first Summer Youth Olympic Games in 2010. Dakar was originally scheduled to host the event in 2022, but the coronavirus pandemic led to its postponement.Africa has hosted several major international sporting events in recent years. South Africa became the first African country to host the FIFA World Cup in 2010, while Morocco will co-host the 2030 tournament with Spain and Portugal. Rwanda hosted the continent's first road cycling world championships last year, and Formula 1 is set to return to Africa with a Grand Prix in Rwanda early next decade.
