articles.body: Fourteen races, fourteen victories and a new world-record to boot. Few athletes in the world have had a more successful 2026 than American track and field star Masai Russell, if any at all. The 26-year-old, though, is not done yet. Ahead of a career-defining, two-year cycle which includes the World Championships in 2027 and 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles, Russell wants to show that she is the “best hurdler to ever exist.” “Just like people are still talking about Usain Bolt and how his records just seem so untouchable,” she says to CNN Sports, “I want people to question the same thing about Masai like, ‘How was she able to do this?’” A dominant season It’s remarkable to think that, this year, Russell stood on the 100m hurdles start line 14 times and, on every occasion, crossed the finish line first. For a sense of that dominance, the last team to go 14-0 at the start of an NFL season was the Carolina Panthers in 2015. Her unbeaten record, however, tells only part of the story. In August, at the Diamond League meeting in Zurich, the Olympic champion broke the world record, clocking a time of 12.09, beating Tobi Amusan’s previous mark by three-hundredths of a second. Russell, though, was hardly surprised. “When I ran 12.09, I was like: Did we not expect this?’” she says. “At the end of the day, it was truly just a blessing to put the work in for so many years and to see the work come out. Regardless of what people have said that I could or couldn’t do, it’s a blessing to see that hard work really does work.” To round off a flawless season, Russell won the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships in 12.22 – the ninth time she went under 12.3 seconds this year. For context, a female athlete has run under 12.3 in the discipline only 49 times in history. Her unbeaten season and world record have earned Russell a nomination for the 2026 Women’s World Athlete of the Year award, which will be presented at the World Athletics Awards in Monaco on November 29. Given the scale of Russell’s extraordinary achievements, it would be foolish to bet against her taking the crown, though she faces stiff competition from athletes including 100m and 200m star Melissa Jefferson-Wooden and European 800m champion Audrey Werro. “I think whatever is meant for me is gonna be,” she says with a wry smile. “But I don’t think anyone did what I did this year in terms of being undefeated, breaking the world record, the times that I was running, all the meet records that I broke. “So, whatever’s going to be is going to be – but I do believe I should win it.” A competitive streak from childhood Russell first began athletics at eight years old, growing up in Upper Marlboro, Maryland, in a fiercely competitive family. Her older brothers, Philip and Devine, played basketball and used track to improve their speed. For their younger sister, they became her first competitors. Some of her earliest athletics memories are of racing them on the street outside their house. “I think my competitive drive definitely came from growing up with my brothers, growing up being the only girl for a long time, just really becoming one of the guys,” Russell recalls. “I think that’s why I was so fast because I was just competing against them, trying to keep up with them.” Russell’s parents, Sharon and Mark Russell, devoted countless hours to helping her pursue her ambitions, providing the support that would underpin her rise to the top of the sport. She recalls endless days spent at track meets where her father would set up a tent and make sure she had food and the support needed to thrive. Similarly, Russell watched her mother balance parenthood with her medical career as a doctor, demonstrating the work ethic that has stayed with her throughout her career. “She definitely showed me what hard work was, what hard work looked like, what being driven and getting it done regardless of how you feel.” Even as a carefree eight-year-old, Russell was developing the drive that would define her career. “I was always having fun, but I had a competitive edge to me. I always just wanted to win. I always wanted to be the best and I just had a different work ethic than everyone else.” Olympic gold and international success The lessons learned and the work ethic instilled by her parents would prove crucial when Russell encountered the first major setbacks in her career. At the 2023 NCAA Championships in Texas, Russell ran a blistering time of 12.32 yet was beaten to the line by Ackera Nugent. Later that summer, having turned professional, Russell qualified for her first World Championships but crashed out at the semifinals after clipping the second hurdle. It was a crushing blow for a supremely talented athlete ready to show what she was made of on the world stage. Painful as it was, Russell saw the setback as part of the process. “I’ve lost a lot, but at the end of the day, you can’t win without losing,” she tells CNN Sports. “You can’t win without failure; you can’t win without having some bumps in the road to make you appreciate why you have won.” The 2024 season also began poorly and winning felt “allergic” to Russell. By her own admission, her times were underwhelming and her first season as a pro athlete threatened to disappoint. Then it all clicked. Russell won her first national title at the US Olympic Trials, setting herself up for the biggest race of her career at the Olympics in Paris. A little over a month later, Russell claimed gold in the women’s 100m hurdles, edging out France’s Cyréna Samba-Mayela by one hundredth of a second. “Crossing the line in Paris, I didn’t know that I won,” Russell recalls. “I looked up and was like ‘I know I got a medal, but which one?’ And when I saw my name come up, I just lost it. “I won the Olympic trials a month before that which was the first time I ever won a national title, and then to come a month later to win my first global title was nothing but a dream, nothing but a freaking dream.” Success on and off the track The emotion of Russell’s Olympic triumph is captured in her YouTube vlog “I WON THE OLYMPICS”, which offers a glimpse of the celebrations shared with her family and team in Paris. Russell’s long-time coach Lonnie Greene has worked with her since her days at the University of Kentucky. In the vlog, a bleary-eyed Greene addresses the camera in the aftermath of her victory. “I told you. I told you you could break the world record, if not be the Olympic champion, and God has allowed that to come to fruition. You will break the world record sooner than you think.” How remarkably prescient that prediction turned out to be. Russell began her YouTube channel in 2017 as a 16-year-old and it’s where she feels the greatest connection with her fans – all 69,300 of them – sharing blogs about her personal and professional life. But Russell’s ambitions extend beyond creating content. With an established following across YouTube and Instagram and her own merchandise line, she is already building a personal brand that can exist independently of her athletics career. “I love to create content and just show my life and show what I’m doing and showcase the things off the track too and showing that I’m bigger than just an athlete,” she says. “So, yeah, the biggest motivation for me is just allowing people to come on this journey with me.” A bright future From racing her brothers on the streets of Upper Marlboro to becoming the fastest female 100-meter hurdler in history, Russell has already come a long way. But the next two years will help determine her legacy in the sport. She will first have a shot at redemption at the World Championships in 2027, followed by the LA Olympic Games in 2028 where she’ll bid to become the first woman in history to win back-to-back 100m hurdles Olympic titles. “I’ve won the Ultimates and checked that off. Won the Olympics and checked that off,” she says. “But now, it’s time to check off a World Championship title and dominate. Continue to show people that I am the best hurdler to ever exist.”

articles.summary: Dave Obelkevich, que ostenta el récord de mayor número de presencias seguidas, es el único corredor que ha terminado todas las ediciones de la carrera disputadas por los cinco distritos
articles.body: En 1973, Dave Obelkevich trotaba por Central Park cuando se cruzó con corredores que llevaban un dorsal. No sabía qué era aquello, pero se unió al grupo y completó casi 10 kilómetros. Aquella experiencia, el maratón de Nueva York, le cautivó y decidió participar en la siguiente edición de la carrera. Al año siguiente, en 1975, tuvo que abandonar por varios episodios de mareo, pero retomó su presencia en 1976 sin ser consciente entonces de que comenzaba un idilio especial con el mítico 'major' de la Gran Manzana. Este domingo, Obelkevich corrió su 50º maratón en Nueva York. Y lo hizo a sus 83 años, en un tiempo de 8.38:26, acompañado de su hija María. El estadounidense ostenta el récord de mayor número de participaciones consecutivas y de más veces que ha completado la carrera. Ha terminado todas las maratones de los cinco distritos que se han celebrado desde 1976. "Correr por el puente Verrazzano-Narrows y a través de barrios que ni siquiera había visitado a pesar de vivir en Nueva York durante años, hizo que el maratón se convirtiera en algo más que una carrera: se convirtió en una celebración anual de la propia ciudad", decía Dave antes de afrontar la carrera. Su mejor tiempo en Nueva York fue en 1982 cuando alcanzó la meta en 2.40:00. "Mi familia está muy orgullosa de mí, y su amor y apoyo significan muchísimo", dijo. "Dejaré que mi cuerpo me diga cuándo se acaba mi racha y espero que eso ocurra dentro de mucho tiempo".

articles.title: Ciara Mageean: Grit and glory - Olympian's career in pictures
articles.summary: After European champion and two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean passed away aged 34, BBC Sport looks back at her career in pictures.
articles.body:
Tributes have been pouring in for European champion and Olympian Ciara Mageean, who passed away on Sunday aged 34.

On the track, she represented Ireland and Northern Ireland with great distinction and she became European 1500m champion in 2024.

Mageean was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025, but continued to be a shining light with her courage.

From her grit and determination to her medal moments, BBC Sport looks back at Mageean's career in pictures.

Gifted athlete whose wit and smile left lasting impression - Mageean obituary

Tributes to 'inspirational' Olympian Ciara Mageean after death at 34

An energetic child who loved to play camogie as well as to run, Mageean had a decorated junior athletics career.

She was third for Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Youth Games in India in 2008, and the following year she won the European Youth Olympic Festival in Finland and was second at the World Youth Championships for Ireland.

Mageean announced herself to senior athletics at the Odyssey Arena by winning the National Senior Indoor title when she was just 15.

In 2010, Mageean was second at the World Junior Championships in Mocton in Canada and she had another breakthrough moment the following year, when she claimed a silver medal at the European Junior Championships in Tallinn.

Mageean missed out on the chance to race at the London Olympics in 2012 through injury, and had surgery on her ankle the following year.

The Portaferry runner bounced back to win the Irish 1500m title in 2014 and things were even better at the European Championships in 2016, when she won a 1500m bronze medal in Amsterdam.

After the highs of a European medal, the Olympics in Rio proved to be disappointing for Mageean after she missed out on a place in the 1500m final.

The following year, she split with long-time coach Jerry Kiernan to work with Steve Vernon in Manchester.

As well as on the track, Mageean often represented Ireland at cross-country level.

Here, her all-or-nothing approach was on show was she emptied the tank at the 2016 European Championships in Italy.

Before Mageean's arrival on the athletics scene, the majority of Ireland's middle-distance record were held by Olympic medallist Sonia O'Sullivan.

Now, she is the Irish record holder in the 800m, 1,000m, both the indoor and outdoor 1500m and the mile.

Mageean finished fourth at the European Championships in 2018, but she went one better the following year at the European Indoors in Glasgow, when she finished in third place behind Laura Muir and Sogia Ennaoui.

There was more disappointment for Mageean at the delayed Tokyo Olympics, which took place in 2021 due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

She injured her calf in the build-up to the Games, and failed to qualify from her heat.

Now coached by Helen Clitheroe, Mageean was back on the podium at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

She finished second behind Muir, who won gold for Scotland, in what was a long-running rivalry that year.

In a successful year, Mageean collected her second European medal in Munich.

Muir again won gold, but Mageean won a silver medal to add to her bronze from 2016.

In another battle with Muir, Mageean came out on top in the 1500m at the Diamond League event in Brussels in 2022.

Not only did she win the race, but her time of 3:56.63 took 3.6 seconds off Sonia O'Sullivan's Irish 1500m record with represented her first sub-four minute run.

A World Championship medal evaded Mageean in her career, but she did finish fourth in the 2023 final in Budapest as Kenya's Faith Kipyegon won gold.

After her bronze in 2016 and silver six years later, Mageean completed the set of European Championship medals when she won a dramatic gold in 2024.

She was boxed in on the final lap behind GB's Georgia Bell and Jemma Reekie, but burst through a gap to win in a time of 4:04.66.

The elation on her face as she crossed the line said everything as she picked up the biggest win of her career.

After she missed the 2024 Paris Olympics through injury, Mageean was diagnosed with stage four cancer the following year.

But just like in her running career, she showed remarkable courage in the face of adversity.

Here, she is presented to the crowd at half-time of the All-Ireland Hurling Final at Croke Park in July.

No matter what she achieved on track, Mageean's connection with her fans and the next generation of runners always shone through.

At the Irish National Championships in July, 400 young athletes from clubs around Ireland joined Mageean in a 'Run with Ciara' celebration in Dublin.

Her smile and enthusiasm will leave a lasting memory.

articles.title: Ciara Mageean, former European 1,500-meter champion, dies at age 34
articles.summary: Ciara Mageean, who won gold in the 1,500 meters at the 2024 European championships, has died.
articles.body: Ciara Mageean, who won gold in the 1,500 meters at the 2024 European championships, has died. She was 34. A statement posted on her Instagram page said she died of cancer on Sunday morning. “At 6:30 a.m. this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones,” the statement said. “A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed.” Mageean won European gold in Rome two years ago, having clinched silver in the 1,500 in Munich in 2022. She placed fourth at the 2023 world championships and represented Ireland in two Olympics. “Athletics Ireland is deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Ciara Mageean,” a statement from Athletics Ireland read. “Ciara was a much-loved and inspirational figure who touched the lives of so many. Her courage, warmth and spirit will leave a lasting legacy.” World Athletics said it was “deeply saddened” by the news, calling her “an inspiration to many, on and off the track.” Australian middle-distance runner Jessica Hull posted a tribute. “There are no words. Just the most beautiful person in every way imaginable,” she wrote on Instagram. “Lucky to have shared some miles with you but even more special to have celebrated milestones at the finish line together, I’m so grateful for every moment, rest easy Ciara.” Sebastian Coe, the president of World Athletics, also paid tribute. “It is with great sadness that we learned of Ciara’s passing this morning at such a young age,” Coe said. “A European champion and inspiration to many, it is a sad day for our sport — her loss will be felt across the athletics community.”

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Indian Olympic Association’s (IOA) Athletes’ Commission election, scheduled for November 3, will not be held after all 10 candidates for the five male and five female positions were declared elected unopposed.In a revised notification issued on Monday, Electoral Officer (RO) Sanjay Kumar Srivastava confirmed that there was only one candidate for each of the 10 positions across the respective categories. Consequently, the election will not serve any purpose, the notification stated.The development follows the withdrawal of nominations by badminton player Kidambi Srikanth and former athlete Sudha Singh. Their withdrawals have left the remaining 10 candidates unopposed.Among the male candidates, shooter Swapnil Suresh Kusale and rower/canoeist Manjeet Singh have been declared unopposed in the medalist category. articles.title: Peleteiro, ante una crítica a su peso: "Me niego a que el comentario de un 'señoro' empañe lo que sentí al verme entrenar"
articles.standfirst: La atleta, que ha sido madre por segunda vez, respondió a un comentario despectivo en redes sobre su cuerpo tras un entrenamiento con el que sigue preparando su regreso al triple
articles.summary: La atleta, que ha sido madre por segunda vez, respondió a un comentario despectivo en redes sobre su cuerpo tras un entrenamiento con el que sigue preparando su regreso al triple
articles.body: Otra vez el cuerpo de las mujeres bajo la lupa. La atleta Ana Peleteiro, bronce olímpica y campeona de Europa de triple, respondió a un comentario despectivo que recibió sobre su peso en redes sociales, tras colgar el vídeo sobre un entrenamiento en el que volvía a saltar, cuatro meses después de dar a luz a su segundo hijo. Así, al mensaje de "pasada de kilos" de un usuario anónimo, Peleteiro aseguró que "quizás por un momento pensó que escribir algo así a una mujer que creó dos vidas, que trabaja, que emprende, que entrena y que se siente tremendamente segura de sí misma, podría generarle algún tipo de complejo, inseguridad o dolor. Pues mira, Tarraco, voy a explicarte algo: Sí, estoy por encima de mi peso de competición. Pero eso no significa que esté "pasada de kilos". Significa que mi cuerpo está en otra etapa, en la que curiosamente me siento más bella, más fuerte, más segura y más empoderada que cuando peso menos de 60 kilos". La atleta continuó diciendo que "mientras tú dedicas parte de tu tiempo a analizar el cuerpo de una mujer que ni siquiera conoces, yo me levanto cada mañana, cuido de mi familia, educo a mis dos hijos, gestiono mis empresas y sigo entrenando y alcanzando un rendimiento físico que desafía muchas de las expectativas que existen alrededor del deporte y la maternidad". Peleteiro insistió en que "los kilos se ganan y se pierden, pero la educación, la inteligencia emocional y el respeto hacia los demás no se consiguen subiéndose a una báscula. Y, por lo visto, son cualidades que a ti te vendría bastante bien empezar a trabajar". La atleta también criticó la opacidad de muchos perfiles en redes sociales que critican y hacen juicios públicos sin mostrar su autoría. "Sí, te voy a exponer públicamente. Porque estoy cansada de que haya personas que crean que, por esconderse detrás de una pantalla y un avatar, tienen impunidad absoluta pata juzgar, humillar y faltar al respeto a los demás". Peleteiro, que continúa con sus entrenamientos para volver a la competición, aseguró que "aún sabiendo que me quedan 5 ó 6 kilos para llegar a mi peso ideal, cuando me vi en este vídeo por primera vez en meses me reconocí y me miré con admiración y felicidad. Me vi fuerte, capaz y cada día más cerca de mi mejor versión. Y me niego a permitir que el comentario de un 'señoro' empañe algo tan bonito como lo que sentí hoy al verme entrenar".

articles.title: Josh Kerr's mile record and Sabastian Sawe's sub-two-hour marathon nominated for World Athletics awards
articles.summary: Josh Kerr's mile world record and Sabastian Sawe breaking the two-hour barrier at the London Marathon are nominated for the moment of the year at the World Athletics Awards.
articles.body:
Josh Kerr's mile world record and Sabastian Sawe breaking the two-hour barrier at the London Marathon have been nominated for the moment of the year at the World Athletics Awards.

Great Britain's Kerr, 29, ran a time of three minutes 42.66 seconds at the London Diamond League in July, smashing the 27-year-old record held by Morocco's Hicham El Guerrouj by almost half a second.

He was cheered on by the home crowd at an electric London Stadium throughout.

In April, Kenya's Sawe, 31, became the first athlete to run a competitive marathon in under two hours in another historic moment for the sport.

Sawe won in a time of one hour 59 minutes 30 seconds, more than one minute faster than the late Kelvin Kiptum's previous marathon record of 2:00:35, set in 2023.

In a remarkable race, Ethiopia's Yomif Kejelcha also broke the two-hour barrier while finishing in second place, and third-placed Jacob Kiplimo also beat the previous world record.

Botswana winning the men's 4x400m relay title in front of a wild home crowd at the world relays was the third nominee.

The awards take place in Monaco on 29 November, with the men's and women's athlete of the year, rising star and coach among the other awards to be presented.

articles.title: A Woman Running the NYC Marathon for Charity Dies 2 Miles from the Finish
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — A young Pennsylvania woman running the New York City Marathon for the first time to raise money for charity collapsed in Central Park, just over two miles from the finish line, and later died.
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — A young Pennsylvania woman running the New York City Marathon for the first time to raise money for charity collapsed in Central Park, just over two miles from the finish line, and later died.

Rachel Apa, 24, of Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, was approaching the 24-mile mark of the 26.2 mile race Sunday when she collapsed, according to the New York Police Department. The city medical examiner's office said Tuesday it was investigating the cause of Apa's death.

Her father told The New York Times that she'd been stricken with rhabdomyolysis, a rare condition in which muscles can break down during exertion, poisoning the body. It was her first marathon, Steve Apa said.

LeBron's KD and Steph Scouting Reports 📋

New York Road Runners, the nonprofit club that stages the race, said in a news release that a bystander administered CPR to Apa, and event medical staffers also did CPR and used a defibrillator. Paramedics arrived and took Apa to a hospital but were unable to save her.

Apa, an industrial-technology product manager and former college field hockey player, had run to raise money for Parkinson's disease in honor of her grandfather.

"It's unfathomable," her father told The Times. He said his daughter, who had just begun a master's program at Charleston Southern University, had been in "perfect health."

Michaela Nicholas was watching the race, cheering on any runners whose names she could discern from their bibs, when Apa passed. Nicholas recalled Tuesday that she called out a message of encouragement, then saw Apa collapse about 15 yards (14 meters) further along the route.

Nicholas, a hospital social worker, said she tried to comfort Apa while two other race spectators performed CPR.

"I just held Rachel's hand and talked to her and told her that she wasn't alone and that she's loved, and I prayed for her," Nicholas, a clinical social worker, said by phone.

The death occurred as the marathon marked 50 years in its five-borough format. Early editions of the race had been run only in Central Park. A record 61,000 runners reached the finish line.

"We are deeply saddened by Rachel's passing following running in Sunday's race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with her family, friends and the entire running community," New York Road Runners said in its statement.

As word of Apa's death spread on Tuesday, money poured into her "Parkinson's Champions" fundraising page, quickly exceeding her $4,000 goal. The fundraiser was sponsored by the Parkinson's Foundation.

On the page, Apa said her grandfather, who had Parkinson's disease and died in 2022, "taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement."

Apa worked for TE Connectivity, which makes various electrical components and electronics. The company was grappling with the news Tuesday and expressed condolences. So did Bucknell University, from which Apa graduated in 2024 with a degree in markets, innovation and design -- and a total of 17 goals for the school's field hockey team.

USA Field Hockey, the sport's governing body, said on social media that "Rachel's impact on the sport and those around her will not be forgotten."
authors: Larry Neumeister and Jennifer Peltz, Associated Press

articles.title: 24-year-old woman dies while running NYC Marathon, reportedly from rhabdomyolysis
articles.summary: Rachel Apa, a former Bucknell University field hockey player, collapsed just more than two miles from the finish line and later died.
articles.body:
A 24-year-old woman from Pennsylvania died after collapsing just more than two miles before the finish line of the New York City Marathon on Sunday.

Rachel Apa, a former Bucknell University field hockey player, collapsed in Central Park while approaching the 24-mile mark of the 26.2-mile race, according to The Associated Press , which cited the the New York Police Department in its Tuesday report.

While the city medical examiner's office said Tuesday, per the AP, that it was investigating the cause of Apa's death, her father, Steve Apa, told The New York Times that the cause of death was rhabdomyolysis, which the Cleveland Clinic classifies as a rare life-threatening condition in which your muscles break down, leading to muscle death.

"When this happens, toxic components of your muscle fibers enter your circulation system and kidneys. This can cause kidney damage," per Cleveland Clinic.

It can stem from overexertion, trauma, medications or an underlying health condition. The NYC Marathon was reportedly Rachel Apa's first marathon, and she was running it for charity, specifically to raise money to fight Parkinson's disease, which her grandfather had when he died in 2022 .

"Choosing a foundation that means something to me was important," Apa wrote in a LinkedIn post months ago . "My grandfather was one of my role models growing up. He taught me to stay active, push my limits and embrace challenges."

Apa's fundraising goal was $4,000. As of Tuesday evening, in the tragic aftermath of her death, her "Parkinson's Champions" fundraising page showed more than $28,000 in donations.

Apa — a Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, native who had just started an MBA program at Charleston Southern University — was working as a product manager for TE Connectivity, an electrical component company.

After Apa collapsed near Mile 24, multiple bystanders — including two people who said they were physicians — took turns giving her CPR, a hospital social worker who was on the scene told the Times.

New York Road Runners, a nonprofit club that puts on the NYC Marathon, said in news release, per the AP , that event medical staffers also performed CPR and used a defibrillator. Once paramedics were on site, they transported Apa to a nearby hospital, but she wasn't able to be saved.

The Times reported, citing timestamped photos and videos shared by spectators, that Apa collapsed at about 1:33 p.m. ET. By 1:40 p.m. ET, a medical crew had arrived, per the Times, which noted that the defibrillator was deployed between 1:41 and 1:50 p.m. ET.

The last time a runner at the marathon died after a medical incident was 2024, according to New York Road Runners.

"We are deeply saddened by Rachel's passing following running in Sunday's race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with her family, friends and the entire running community," New York Road Runners said in its statement, per the AP.

At Bucknell, Apa appeared in 63 field hockey games, making 42 starts and posting 17 goals and six assists. She was a two-time member of the Patriot League Academic Honor Roll.

articles.title: Four decades after his death, how Jalandhar keeps the spirit of Surjit Singh Randhawa alive
articles.summary: Jalandhar: Every city has its legends. In hockey-loving Jalandhar, Surjit Singh Randhawa is more than a legend. He remains a presence.
articles.body: Jalandhar: Every city has its legends. In hockey-loving Jalandhar, Surjit Singh Randhawa is more than a legend. He remains a presence.His name greets visitors at the stadium named after him, echoes through the roads leading to the venue and lives on in an academy that continues to produce international players, six of whom are currently part of the Indian team, including captain Harmanpreet Singh.More than four decades after his death in a road accident in 1984, Surjit — a World Cup winner, an Olympian and an Arjuna Award recipient — remains woven into the sporting fabric of the region.The ongoing Asian Champions Trophy here has brought the spotlight back on the man widely regarded as one of India’s greatest full-backs and penalty-corner specialist. It was Surjit’s equaliser against Pakistan in the 1975 World Cup final paved the way for Ashok Kumar’s title-winning goal.But for those who knew him, Surjit was not merely a hockey star. He was a teammate, a mentor, a friend and, perhaps most importantly, a symbol of what Punjab hockey once was and still aspires to be.Former India captain Ajit Pal Singh, who was India’s captain in 1975, remembers Surjit as one of the pillars of that golden generation. “He was a dependable defender, a penalty-corner specialist and a fighter to the core. As captain, I always had complete faith in him as a teammate,” said Ajit Pal.Yet his journey began in far more humble surroundings.Brigadier Harcharan Singh, another Olympian and three-time World Cup medallist, first saw Surjit as a teenager at a village tournament in 1969. Recognising his talent, he helped the youngster gain admission to Sports College, Jalandhar.Within a few years, the boy who almost missed out on a place at the college established himself as one of the world’s finest defenders. What separated Surjit from others, according to those who played with him, was his relentless work ethic.“Surjit imposed a very disciplined routine on himself. After finishing regular training with the team, he would put in another four or five hours of individual practice,” Harcharan recalled.That dedication transformed him into a player opponents feared and goalkeepers dreaded.Former India goalkeeper Alloysius Edwards never had the chance to play against Surjit but grew up hearing stories about the Punjab legend’s ferocious hitting power.“I once heard from a goalkeeper playing for JCT that he fractured a finger while attempting to stop one of Surjit’s penalty-corner strikes in an era before modern protective equipment became standard,” said Edwards, who represented India at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics and currently coaches Punjab & Sind Bank’s hockey team in Jalandhar.His reputation as a penalty-corner expert became so great that many in Punjab draw a direct line from Prithipal Singh to Surjit Singh and then to present-day India captain Harmanpreet, another defender who is equally lethal from penalty corners.Yet, those who knew him insist his greatness extended beyond hockey.Perhaps Surjit’s greatest contribution came after his playing days ended. What could have faded into history has instead evolved into an institution. For former India captain and Punjab sports administrator Pargat Singh, preserving those memories is precisely why the institutions carrying Surjit’s name remain relevant today.“The younger generation may not know much about him, so we are trying to keep his memories alive. Ultimately, he is part of our history. If we can pass that history on to the next generation, it can inspire and motivate young players,” said Pargat, who served as Director of Sports for Punjab for approximately seven years.That effort is evident across Jalandhar.While the stadium that bears Surjit’s name is hosting an international tournament, Surjit Memorial Hockey Tournament remains one of India’s most respected domestic competitions and Surjit Hockey Academy continues to shape future internationals.The academy, which houses around 100 trainees, has become one of Punjab’s premier hockey nurseries.Players still recount tales of his World Cup heroics, ferocious penalty corners and remarkable understanding of the game. One trainee, Gursimranpreet Singh, recalled an incident in which Surjit challenged officials over the positioning of the goalposts during an international match and was ultimately proven right.Along with the Surjit Hockey Society, which continues to organise the annual memorial tournament, the academy has ensured that Surjit’s influence extends far beyond his playing days.The results are visible in Punjab’s continued production line of talent. Players such as Harmanpreet Singh, Manpreet Singh, Hardik Singh, Mandeep Singh and Jarmanpreet Singh are the latest products of a hockey belt stretching across Jalandhar, Batala and Amritsar.To many former internationals, that pipeline is Surjit’s greatest legacy.His wife, Chanchal Surjit Singh, a former captain of the Indian women’s hockey team, sums it up best.“There is nothing more I can add after seeing all the love people still have for him. He was a legend and one of the kindest souls. To see an international tournament taking place in a stadium named after him is very special,” said Chanchal, 74.Ram Pratap, one of Surjit’s closest friends who was travelling with him when the fatal car crash occurred near Kartarpur, remembers him as much for his character as for his achievements.“Surjit was a legend and perhaps the best full-back in the world. But more importantly, he was a wonderful human being. That’s why people still remember him with so much affection,” he said.To many in Punjab hockey, memories of Surjit the player have endured because they are inseparable from memories of Surjit the person.The reverence extends beyond memories. A stadium in Jalandhar bears his name, while his native village, Dakhla, in Gurdaspur district, was renamed Surjit Singh Wala, a rare honour that underlines the impact he had on Punjab and Indian hockey.The Government Sports College, which was later renamed the Government Arts and Sports College in 1977, also continues to celebrate its sporting heroes and preserve its legacy.“Plans are underway to name the boys’ hostel after Surjit Singh, while honour boards and a dedicated alumni wall will ensure that future generations remember the contributions of our Olympians and international players,” said principal Ranbir Singh, a former national hockey player who played for Namdhari XI alongside Sardar Singh.Most athletes are remembered for what they achieved. Surjit is remembered for what he continues to inspire.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: World Junior Ice Hockey Championships: Canada bars Russia and Belarus from tournament
articles.summary: Canada will not ​let ice hockey players from Russia or Belarus take part ‌in the World Junior Championships next month.
articles.body:
Canada will not ​let ice hockey players from Russia or Belarus take part ‌in the World Junior Championships next month.

Russia had been suspended from competing in International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) events since the country invaded Ukraine in February 2022, but last week the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) overturned the ban .

The IIHF has reaffirmed its "disagreement" with the decision, adding in a statement that the situation and implications for upcoming events will be closely monitored.

"The global impact of the decision made by the Cas Panel and the challenges it creates for all involved were significantly underestimated," an IIHF statement said.

Ukraine's ice hockey federation expressed "deep outrage" at Russia being allowed to compete in international events again.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific war in Ukraine, as ​long as that's going on, there will be none of ​those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," Canada prime minister Mark Carney said.

"So, if you're ‌asking ⁠specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

The World Junior Ice Hockey Championships are scheduled to run from 26 December to 5 January.

Oleg Stepanov, the ​Russian ⁠ambassador to Canada, said: "It is regrettable that Carney's office is ⁠bringing ​politics even into junior hockey, which ​is meant to unite, not divide."

National ice ​hockey federations in ​Norway, Denmark, ⁠Sweden and the Czech Republic also said on Tuesday they would refuse to play Russia at next year's men's ​Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany.

articles.title: Could Hyrox's Olympic ambition spell the end for triathlon?
articles.summary: BBC Sport speaks to several triathletes about what World Triathlon's Hyrox partnership means for the future of the sport.
articles.body:
"Our biggest concern is that they're not just here to take part, they're here to take over."

British triathlete Max Stapley first saw the news on Instagram. Last week, World Triathlon announced it was partnering with Hyrox - the fitness craze which combines running with exercise stations.

The agreement means Hyrox becomes a recognised discipline within World Triathlon. And now it sits under a recognised international federation, it could be eligible for inclusion at the Olympics and Paralympics.

It is too late for the Los Angeles 2028 Games but is there room for both hybrid racing and triathlon to feature at a future Olympics? Or could one replace the other?

For triathlon, a sport which has been in the Olympics since 2000, and has long-established professional circuits, its athletes are questioning whether they'll reap any rewards from this partnership - or even, whether it could "kill" the sport altogether.

Stapley, who spoke to BBC Sport from a training camp in Thailand, was having dinner with friends when his phone started pinging with news of the proposals and reaction to them.

"I was like, hold on a minute, what's this?", said Stapley.

"We don't even get an early notification, we found out on Instagram".

The post read , external : 'Hyrox x World Triathlon are officially introducing 'Hybrid Racing' as a new discipline within the World Triathlon family.'

Sophie Evans - who won gold as part of England's Commonwealth Games mixed relay team in Birmingham in 2022 - said she was "surprised" to receive the news like that.

"I'm not actually against it being part of World Triathlon. It's more the fact we were blindsided, it's just like it's here," she added.

Stapley accused World Triathlon of not caring about its athletes because he did not receive any communication from his sport's governing body prior to and after the announcement was made.

"They have no respect for us," he said. "They don't even contact us like 'hey, do you guys actually care about this, or what do you think?'"

In response, a World Triathlon spokesperson told BBC Sport: "The World Triathlon Executive Board approved the partnership. The board includes representatives of the World Triathlon Athletes' Committee elected by their peers.

"Athlete representatives are involved in every executive board discussion, and their voice is always heard.

"The announcement was communicated through the same procedures followed for all World Triathlon releases."

World Triathlon says the partnership is designed to "benefit the entire World Triathlon movement", , external with new opportunities to engage athletes and audiences, and a stronger platform to grow triathlon and multisport from grassroots to elite level.

European champion Roksana Slupek, of Poland, said she was "not against the idea", but wanted more information.

"What's the benefit for us, for triathlon? It's nothing against Hyrox," said Slupek.

However, Stapley called the move an "attack on our whole existence" and is concerned that World Triathlon could direct attention and resources towards Hyrox's Olympic ambition - at the expense of his own sport.

"How does Hyrox grow triathlon? If anything they've killed triathlon," he said, while also suggesting brands would rather get in early with Hyrox athletes before they potentially appear at an Olympics.

"Sponsorships have reduced because there's no visibility on TV, you have to pay to watch us.

"We are triathletes that do the short distance, which is the Olympic distance, and we've trained all our lives for it.

"There's no swimming, there's no biking, it's indoors. [Hyrox] has got nothing to do [with triathlon]".

"It seems like our sport's gone, 'no worries, come along, use our structure, use our access to the International Olympic Committee, and perhaps take our space'.

"We've got an opportunity to win medals in Los Angeles [at the 2028 Olympics], but will we have it further down the track?"

Evans said that while triathlon was an "established" Olympic sport, that has provided high quality racing since its introduction to the Games 26 years ago, this new partnership has introduced a "level of uncertainty".

"A lot of the resistance has come from athletes, because you don't know," she added.

A World Triathlon spokesperson told BBC Sport, it is continuing to "increase its focus and involvement in the Olympic and Paralympic families" and that it is in the "planning phase" for Brisbane 2032, adding that "triathlon is, and will remain, at the heart of everything we do".

BBC Sport approached Hyrox for comment, but they referred us to the statements made by World Triathlon.

Can triathlon and Hybrid racing co-exist?

Sam Dickinson - who won an Olympic triathlon bronze in Paris as part Team GB's relay quartet - can see why the move makes sense but wants more clarity.

"It's trying to get people active not from an elite side but from a participation side," Dickinson told BBC Sport.

"So in that sense it does make sense that as a multi-sport it comes under the World Triathlon umbrella.

"But it's early days, we don't have any of the bread and butter of exactly what's going on."

And there lies the crux of the problem - the lack of clarity has fuelled speculation about what the future holds.

World Triathlon does have other disciplines in its remit, such as Aquathlon and duathlon.

BBC Sport has been told that 'Fitness Racing' was first included as a discipline in the World Triathlon Constitution in October 2025, a move supported by the majority of the governing body's National Federations.

A World Triathlon spokesperson added that the partnership provides opportunities to 'reach new audiences' through collaborating with global partners.

Founded in 2017, Hyrox's popularity has continued to grow rapidly. A total of 1.5m athletes took part during the 2025/26 season - up from 650,000 the year before - with participation projected to surpass 2m in the current season.

British Triathlon, one of World Triathlon's national federations, told BBC Sport it recognises "World Triathlon's work to grow, develop and strengthen the sport of triathlon, multi-sport and its community", but is waiting to hear the "full operational, governance and commercial framework" for the partnership.

articles.title: PV Sindhu returns to world top six after four years; here's how India's star rebuilt her ranking
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: PV Sindhu's resurgence on the international badminton circuit has received another significant boost, with the two-time Olympic medallist
articles.body: NEW DELHI: PV Sindhu's resurgence on the international badminton circuit has received another significant boost, with the two-time Olympic medallist climbing to world No. 6 in the latest women's singles rankings, her highest position since December 2022.The 31-year-old Indian shuttler has made an impressive return to the top six following a productive season on the BWF World Tour, highlighted by two titles and multiple deep runs at major tournaments.Sindhu's latest ranking improvement comes on the back of her triumph at the Hylo Open in Germany, where she defeated Denmark's Line Kjaersfeldt 21-12, 21-14 in the women's singles final on Sunday. The victory marked her second BWF World Tour title of the season and continued the momentum she had built over the preceding weeks.Her return to the top six is particularly significant given the challenges she has faced in recent seasons. The former world champion has gradually rediscovered her consistency, competing against a strong field featuring both established stars and a new generation of women's singles players.ALSO READ: PV Sindhu sees new wave in Indian badminton: 'Initially, there was a gap, but now we have these girls'Two titles and multiple final-four finishesSindhu's climb in the rankings has been driven by a series of encouraging performances this season.She began her title-winning campaign with the Japan Open in July before adding the Hylo Open crown in Germany. In between, she reached the final of the French Open, where she finished runner-up to world No. 1 An Se Young.The Indian also made semifinal appearances at the Malaysia Open and Australian Open, further strengthening her position among the leading players on the circuit.Her recent performances have also helped her secure a place in the season-ending BWF World Tour Finals, scheduled to take place in Hangzhou, China, from December 9 to 13. Sindhu is fifth in the HSBC Race to Finals rankings, with the top eight players qualifying for the elite tournament.She will be looking to repeat her success from 2018, when she won the prestigious season-ending competition.'31 is the new 21': Sindhu on competing at the topSindhu has attributed her resurgence to consistent performances, patience and better management of her physical condition."I'm happy that I've climbed into the top six now. I just feel that if you keep doing well, you automatically start winning and your ranking also comes up. If you perform well and win tournaments, you don't have to think only about the ranking. It will automatically improve," she said.The Indian star, who has competed against several generations of leading women's singles players, remains confident about returning to the very top."Absolutely. Why not? If you take care of your body, definitely yes. It's just about how you take care of your body. A lot of athletes are playing in their 30s, 31s and 32s, and there have been many who were at the top at that age. So, why not get back to the top again? I'm getting there, and I am there."Sindhu also underlined the importance of managing her tournament schedule rather than playing continuously."I'm not young anymore, but you know, 31 is the new 21. So I need to take care of my body, isn't it?"With her ranking back among the world's top six and a place secured at the BWF World Tour Finals, Sindhu's latest run represents an encouraging chapter in her bid to re-establish herself among the very best in women's badminton.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Harmanpreet, Shilanand lead India's goal fest as hosts thrash South Korea 8-1, set ACT final against Japan
articles.summary: India produced a breathtaking attacking display to storm into the final of the Asian Champions Trophy 2026, thrashing South Korea 8-1 in the semi-final in
articles.body: India produced a breathtaking attacking display to storm into the final of the Asian Champions Trophy 2026, thrashing South Korea 8-1 in the semi-final in Mohali on Wednesday. The hosts underlined their title credentials with a dominant performance, scoring eight goals to maintain their unbeaten run in the tournament and move one step closer to lifting the trophy.Shilanand Lakra and Dilpreet Singh scored twice each, while Harmanpreet Singh, Sukhjeet Singh, Angad Bir Singh and Vivek Sagar Prasad also got on the scoresheet as India overwhelmed the South Korean defence. India will now face Japan in the final after the latter defeated Malaysia in the first semi-final. South Korea, meanwhile, will take on Malaysia in the bronze-medal match.Shilanand, Harmanpreet lead India's early chargeIndia made an aggressive start and took the lead in the fourth minute through Shilanand Lakra. Dilpreet Singh did the hard work with a superb run down the left before setting up Shilanand, who applied the finishing touch to put the hosts ahead.South Korea, however, found an equaliser against the run of play in the ninth minute. Song delivered a pass from the right, and Han Sangjun directed the ball past goalkeeper Suraj Karkera to make it 1-1.The equaliser did little to slow India down. The hosts responded almost immediately, earning a penalty corner after a backstick infringement. Captain Harmanpreet Singh stepped up and unleashed a powerful drag-flick to restore India's lead. The goal was briefly referred for a check over the trap during the penalty corner, but the TV umpire allowed it to stand. It was Harmanpreet's 10th goal of the tournament.India continued to pile pressure on the visitors and doubled their advantage in the 13th minute. Harmanpreet's drag-flick was initially saved by the South Korean goalkeeper, but Shilanand reacted quickest to the rebound and converted from close range to complete his brace.India run riot with four goals in second quarterThe hosts carried their momentum into the second quarter, with Sukhjeet Singh making it 4-1 in the 19th minute. Sanjay provided the pass, and Sukhjeet displayed excellent control before turning and producing a superb no-look finish.India struck again just a minute later. Dilpreet capitalised on a poor pass from South Korea, combined with Angad Bir Singh through a quick one-two and calmly slotted the ball past the goalkeeper to extend the lead to 5-1.Dilpreet then produced one of the standout moments of the match in the 25th minute. Harmanpreet picked him out with a long pass, and the Indian forward took a first-time shot from a tight angle to beat the goalkeeper and make it 6-1. South Korea struggled to contain India's attacking movements, with the hosts finding spaces almost at will.Angad and Vivek add to South Korea's miseryIndia added their seventh goal in the 36th minute through Angad Bir Singh. Jarmanpreet Singh delivered a pass from the right, and Angad got a crucial touch to redirect the ball into the net. The goal further highlighted India's attacking depth, with multiple players contributing to the rout.The hosts had opportunities to increase their advantage in the third quarter but were unable to find another breakthrough. They also earned a penalty corner following a successful review, but Amandeep Lakra's effort was saved by the South Korean goalkeeper.South Korea showed slightly more intent in possession during the final quarter, but India remained in control. Harmanpreet came close to creating another opportunity with a superb aerial pass that bypassed the entire Korean defence, although Angad's reverse-hit attempt missed the target.India eventually completed the eight-goal rout in the 54th minute. Vivek Sagar Prasad made a brilliant diagonal run, controlled the ball and unleashed a reverse-hit shot. The effort went in after taking a deflection off the goalkeeper's pads, sealing an emphatic 8-1 victory for the hosts.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Sports Owners Got Very Little for Their Money in Midterm Elections
articles.summary: Democrats will hold at least 54 Senate seats.
articles.body:
Tuesday's midterm elections provided a sweeping win for Democrats across the country, and for most of the professional sports team owners who poured more than $100 million into the races, a poor return on investment.

The vast majority of dollars sports owners spent on the midterms went to Republicans, according to a Front Office Sports analysis of Federal Election Commission filings for the principal owners of teams in the NFL, NBA, WNBA, MLB, NHL, MLS, and NWSL.

On Tuesday, Democrats took control of the House and the Senate, flipping at least seven Senate seats from Republican control. Many of the Republicans in battleground Senate races, including candidates running in Ohio, Texas, Maine, and North Carolina, received hundreds of thousands of dollars in support from pro sports team owners.

Of the top 25 donors to the midterms among sports owners, only three of them gave mostly or entirely to Democrats: Seattle Seahawks owner Vinod Khosla ($2.09 million), Chicago Stars owner Laura Ricketts ($316,500), and Atlanta Hawks and United owner Arthur Blank ($315,500).

The largest donor among team owners was Dallas Mavericks owner Miriam Adelson, a major player in Republican politics thanks to her roughly $50 billion net worth stemming from her late husband's casino business. After giving $100 million to President Donald Trump in 2024, she donated more than $67 million to Republicans this cycle. Also on Tuesday, ESPN reported Adelson has sold controlling ownership of the Mavs to her daughter and son-in-law.

Some of the biggest surprises of the midterms received little to no support from team owners.

In South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Republican Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, FOS found no recorded donations from principal team owners to either candidate. A handful of owners did contribute to Lindsey Graham before his death in July; Athletics minority owner Ken Jeong, a comedian and actor who joined a $70 million investment round in the team this summer, donated $6,000 to Andrews.

Mississippi's Senate race, where Democrat Scott Colom currently leads Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 43 votes with ballots still outstanding, also attracted little fanfare. Los Angeles Kings and Galaxy owner Philip Anschutz and San Francisco Giants owner Charles B. Johnson donated to Hyde-Smith's principal campaign committee, while no owners gave to Colom.

In 2018, the Office of the Commissioner of Major League Baseball donated $5,000 to Hyde-Smith, but MLB requested the money be returned after backlash to Hyde-Smith saying she would be willing to attend a "public hanging" if a supporter invited her. Johnson also donated to Hyde-Smith and eventually requested a refund after calling her comments " stupid ."eventually requested a refund after calling her comments "stupid."

Other big winners from Tuesday including Michigan's Abdul Ed-Sayed, Maine's Troy Jackson, and Iowa's Josh Turek took in $0 of direct donations to their campaign committees from principal team owners, according to FEC records.

Meanwhile, candidates in key Senate races that did receive money from the sports world mostly struck out.

Team owners gave more than $350,000 to Republican Senate candidates in nine battleground states, almost six times what they gave to their Democratic opponents, according to FOS analysis of principal campaign committee donations. The filings show more than 15 team owners gave to re-elect Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, and more than a dozen owners donated to support Jon Husted in Ohio. Both candidates conceded their races Tuesday night.

As of Wednesday morning, eight of the nine battleground states analyzed by FOS —Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas—all went blue. The race in Alaska has not yet been called.

Not all Republican donations by sports team owners went to losing candidates. Tennessee Rep. Matt Van Epps won reelection with the help of donors including Browns and Columbus soccer owners Jimmy and Dee Haslam, and Nashville Predators owner and former Tennessee Gov. Bill Haslam. Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection following donations from Broncos owner Rob Walton, Dee Haslam, and Magic co-owner Richard "Dick" Devos.

Speaker of the House Mike Johnson from Louisiana, who announced on Wednesday he will not run for House Minority Leader, received donations from owners including Arizona Diamondbacks owner Ken Kendrick, Athletics and San Jose Earthquakes owner John Fisher, and Boston Bruins owner Jeremy Jacobs. Anschutz was the single largest donor to Johnson's leadership PAC with more than $500,000.

On the other side of the aisle, Blank contributed to New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez's successful reelection campaign. 76ers and Devils co-owner David Blitzer donated to Colorado Sen. John Hickenlooper's reelection, and a number of owners including Blitzer, Washington Capitals, Wizards, and Mystics owner Ted Leonsis, and Vancouver Whitecaps owner Steve Luczo contributed to groups supporting Virginia Sen. Mark Warner or his principal campaign committee.

Padres Pitcher: El-Sayed 'A Great Progressive Voice'

In Michigan, at least 10 owners donated to Republican Mike Rogers , combining to give more than $50,000 to his principal campaign committee. New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, meanwhile, gave $100,000 to the Great Lakes Conservatives Fund, a PAC running ads on Rogers's behalf.

While El-Sayed received no support from principal team owners, he did receive a $1,250 campaign donation from Padres pitcher Lucas Giolito. As election results were coming in Tuesday night showing El-Sayed was likely to prevail, Giolito explained his support to FOS .

"I've been very fortunate in my career. I feel it's very important to give back when this country has given me so much," Giolito told FOS . "When I saw Abdul's movement growing in Michigan, I just wanted to throw some support his way. His platform and policy aligns with my values, and although I don't live in Michigan, I believe he'll be a great progressive voice in the US senate."

Cooper Flips North Carolina With Support From Silver, $30K From Owners

Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper decisively beat Republican Michael Whatley by roughly 20 points to take back another Senate seat for Democrats.

Both Cooper and Whatley received around $30,000 from sports owners, with the former governor slightly ahead.

Blitzer, Seattle Kraken owner Samantha Holloway, and Pacers and Fever owner Herb Simon donated directly to Cooper's principal campaign committee. New York Giants chairman Steve Tisch, Seahawks owner Khosla, and Philadelphia Flyers governor Dan Hilferty also donated to Cooper through joint fundraising committees.

Additionally, NBA commissioner Adam Silver gave to Cooper, his affiliated joint fundraising committee, and the North Carolina Democratic Party. Silver and Cooper crossed paths when the NBA brought the All-Star Game to Charlotte in 2019; the league had relocated the 2017 All-Star Game out of North Carolina due to the state's controversial "bathroom bill" signed by Cooper's predecessor, which was rolled back by the now Senator-elect. Silver also donated to Cooper's gubernatorial reelection campaign in 2020.

Whatley received support from a group of prolific Republican donors including Magic owners Dick and Dan DeVos, Broncos owner Rob Walton, Giants owner Johnson, and Anschutz.

State-level races went no better for Republicans, with Democrats flipping governor's mansions in Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Georgia, and Nevada and clinching a majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years .

In New York, Knicks and Rangers owner James Dolan bet big on Republican gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman, who fell far short Tuesday night. Incumbent Democrat Kathy Hochul leads Blakeman by more than 20 points with 88% of the vote reported.

Dolan had previously been a major backer of Hochul, pouring $700,000 to support her 2022 campaign through a super PAC controlled by Madison Square Garden. This cycle, however, he flipped his support to Blakeman. Dolan directed millions to Blakeman's campaign and affiliated PACs, according to a New York Times analysis , and also hosted a fundraiser for Blakeman during a Knicks preseason game.

Ohio gubernatorial Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy also lost after receiving significant support from sports owners in his home state. Cleveland Guardians owner Paul Dolan, Cincinnati Reds owner Robert Castellini, Cincinnati Bengals owner Mike Brown, Cleveland Browns owners Jimmy and Dee Haslam, and Cleveland Cavaliers owner Dan Gilbert all gave to Ramaswamy, FOIAball reported .

Democratic nominee Amy Acton defeated Ramaswamy by roughly 8 points . Ramaswamy came under fire late in the campaign for running an ad featuring Acton's estranged mother who lost custody of Acton over allegations that her husband sexually abused Acton.
